This page is the landing point for KE's posture toward open scholarly standards — what the platform commits to, what ships today, and what is honestly still on the way. Read it if you are a librarian or data curator asking whether exports will outlive the platform, an institutional reviewer or grants office looking for the interoperability story, an environment administrator deciding what your knowledge environment inherits without configuration, or a research team weighing the platform for a future project. Each section deepens progressively; the table is the heart of the page. Standards adoption matters here because three things are true at once. Interoperability with the FAIR data ecosystem — findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable — is non-negotiable for an academic platform. Research data will outlast the platform that produced it, so the formats it lives in must be readable by tools the platform does not control. And scholarly citation depends on identifiers, vocabularies, and packaging that the wider research community already trusts — an identifier only the platform understands is not a citation, it is a private bookmark. Standards are the shared foundation; a research team's interpretation rides on top of it. Voice, vocabulary, and scholarly choices stay specific to each knowledge environment — the standards layer is what makes those choices legible outside the environment's own walls.

The platform distinguishes four maturity tiers, so that "we comply with X" never has to be read on faith: Built — shipped in production code and exercised by at least one feature you can see today. Removing it would break something visible. Active — partially implemented and in real use. You can configure against the standard, but the full export or rendering pipeline is not yet complete end to end. Validated — the platform has researched the standard, committed to its shape in a recorded design decision, and can defend the choice in front of a partner — but no implementation ships yet. Validated means committed, not built. Deferred — recognised as relevant; no commitment and no implementation until a research project or a partner contract makes the need concrete. Listed openly so the absence is visible rather than silent. The selection of standards in the table is itself deliberate. KE's scope spans text, structured data, geographic and temporal modelling, persistent identity, accessibility, and data protection — each with its own established body of standards. The table covers the standards the platform has committed to, surveyed in depth, or recognised as a near-future need. Standards outside this scope (medical imaging's DICOM, financial reporting's XBRL, music encoding's MEI) are not listed; if a future research project requires one, the same sequence applies before it enters this table — research first, then a recorded decision, then implementation. A full TEI export of published records is committed but not yet built. May be added for a narrow harvesting endpoint if a partner institution requires it. A full, recorded WCAG 2.2 AA audit has not yet been performed — Active here means real but partial, not certified. The platform's activity log redacts personal data before anything is written, and the log is tamper-evident — each entry is cryptographically chained to the one before it. Active Pleiades Gazetteer of ancient places On the platform's accepted standards list as a place-identity authority; live lookup is not yet built. Validated ORCID Researcher identity On the platform's accepted standards list; planned for researcher identity and contribution attribution on published work. Validated DOI / Crossref / DataCite Persistent identifiers; bibliographic registration Published records are designed to carry a stable, citable identity against which a DOI can be registered with an external agency. The platform does not mint DOIs itself. Validated

Compliance here is structural, not declarative. Any platform can claim conformance on a slide deck; what matters is whether drift from a declared standard fails visibly or hides as documentation rot. KE's posture is that drift should fail loudly — when data is saved, when a record is published, or when it is exported. Five mechanisms carry that posture: Standards declarations on fields. Fields in an environment's data model can declare the standards they conform to — a TEI element, a CIDOC-CRM class, an IIIF presentation shape. The declaration travels with the data through publication and export, so an outside reader can see what the data claims about itself without guessing. A vetted standards list. Environments declare conformance only against standards the platform has actually surveyed. Adding a new standard follows a fixed sequence: research first, then a recorded decision, then implementation. A coverage matrix. Every surveyed standard is mapped against every family of concepts the platform models, cell by cell, so each conformance statement traces back to recorded evidence rather than to a slogan. Validation at publication time. Before a published record's export goes out, automated checks refuse any claim of full coverage of a standard that the platform cannot actually validate. These checks run today for citation, image-annotation, and linked-data shapes; machine-runnable validation suites for TEI and CIDOC are planned, and they gate any public conformance claim for those two standards. Gates in the development process. Automated checks keep environment-specific vocabulary out of shared platform code, so the conformance machinery every environment relies on stays identical for all of them.

If you are a researcher. Your knowledge environment inherits scholarly citation and standards-grade export commitments without any configuration on your part. Your interpretive decisions are preserved when your source data is re-imported, citations render in your environment's chosen style, and the export formats in the table above are how your data is designed to travel to your institutional repository. See Citation Integrity and DOI Safety for the citation guarantee and Voice and Vocabulary for how your wording stays yours. If you are an environment administrator. Standards and Citations covers what your environment gets without configuration, what you can configure — citation style, vocabulary grounding against external authorities, standards declarations — and how your data exports. Vocabulary Grounding carries the operational steps. If you are a librarian, data curator, or institutional reviewer. The table above and the Pending and deferred section together are the honest inventory: what ships, what is committed, and what is recognised but not started. The versioning rules below explain how an export made today stays legible in ten years. If you are a research team evaluating the platform. The maturity tags tell you what you can rely on today versus what is planned. If a standard your project requires is at Validated or Deferred, ask the platform operator for an explicit timeline; the openly recorded gap is the basis for that conversation.

When a research team's environment is set up, the adoption decisions in the table are already made. The environment's fields can declare conformance against the accepted standards list; its published records flow through the same publication pipeline as every other environment's; its vocabulary can ground against the same external authorities — Wikidata and PeriodO — as everyone else's. What the environment configures is layered on top: citation style, vocabulary grounding choices, standards declarations, and its own voice and wording. The foundation is shared; the interpretation belongs to the research team. The practical sequence for a new environment: The environment's concept families are configured from the platform's shared field types. Fields can optionally declare which accepted standards they conform to. Vocabulary grounding — Wikidata for entities, PeriodO for periods — is offered as a guided workflow; the environment administrator reviews proposed matches and confirms the ones that fit. A citation style is selected; the choice flows into every surface where the platform renders citations. Published records flow through the shared publication pipeline. As each export format — JSON-LD, RO-Crate, TEI — reaches Built maturity, it becomes available to every environment at once, with no environment-specific code.

documents.t: No single standard covers everything a research collection needs to express. A place record may carry CIDOC-CRM for cultural-heritage modelling, GeoSPARQL for geometry, schema.org markup for search-engine visibility, Pleiades or Wikidata identifiers for external identity, and a JSON-LD context for serialisation — all at once. The platform's shared definitions are designed around composition: a single definition can declare conformance with several standards at once, and the export pipeline is designed to carry each conformance statement alongside the others. When two standards model the same thing with different shapes — a historical period as a CIDOC-CRM period, a Dublin Core period of time, or a SKOS concept — the platform is designed to express each shape from the same underlying record rather than picking one and discarding the others. A researcher does not have to choose which standard their data complies with. When a standard is silent on something the platform needs to express, the gap is recorded explicitly, and the extension lives as a clearly separate field rather than as a falsified conformance claim.

Standards themselves evolve. TEI is on P5; IIIF Presentation is on 3.0; CIDOC-CRM is on 7.1.3; WCAG is on 2.2. KE pins each adoption to a specific version of the standard, recorded with the adoption decision, and exported data is designed to carry that version pin in its conformance statements — so a future reader can resolve the exact specification the data was produced against. This is what keeps a 2026 export legible in 2036: the version pin is the contract.

Items where adoption is recognised as relevant but not yet committed, or committed but not yet finished — listed openly so the absence is visible: Darwin Core — no current research project requires biodiversity-grade modelling of taxa and specimens. It becomes a candidate when a project with specimen-level or species-level data joins the platform and the evidence review supports adoption. ICU (Unicode collation and folding) — sorting and accent handling currently use per-field folding rules over the database's and the search engine's built-in facilities. ICU becomes a candidate when a project needs Unicode-grade case or accent folding beyond those facilities, or when a partner requires ICU conformance in a contract. OpenAPI — GraphQL is the platform's primary interface. OpenAPI becomes a candidate if a partner institution requires it for automated harvesting of a specific endpoint. Full WCAG 2.2 AA audit — the accessibility controls ship today; the recorded end-to-end audit is queued until the public reading surface is stable, so that the audit measures a fixed target rather than a moving one. Until that audit is recorded, the platform does not present itself as WCAG-certified. CIDOC / Linked Art validation suites — machine-runnable validation tests are a precondition the platform set for itself: no public claim of CIDOC conformance until they pass. The suites are not yet written; holding the claim until they pass is deliberate. TEI conformance bundle — a runnable, version-pinned validation bundle is planned once published exports are stable enough to validate against TEI. When complete, it will be published alongside this overview. These gaps are recorded openly so that anyone evaluating the platform can read what it does not yet do alongside what it does. A known conformance gap beats an unverified conformance claim.

You operate one knowledge environment on a multi-tenant platform. This area of the documentation tells you what you configure, where each control lives, and how to verify changes reach the surfaces you expect. Read this if you are onboarding a new environment, revising a configuration after researcher feedback, or auditing what your environment is doing. The platform ships generic. Your job is to shape four things: how the platform speaks, who can do what, what data comes in, and what the platform records about how it is being used.

Ordered by how often a typical administrator uses each. Voice and vocabulary substitution — the words the platform uses across every researcher-facing surface. Maturity: Active. Limit: scoped to platform-emitted wording; never rewrites researcher-authored content. See Voice and Vocabulary. Permissions panel — contributors, role composition, project rules, ownership transfers, and the audit trail. Maturity: Active. Limit: the permissions that make up each standard role are fixed; custom roles compose from the same building blocks. See Permissions Panel. Data import wizard — guided review of import proposals in the administration interface, across Excel (.xlsx), MySQL, CSV bundle, and Coda sources. The platform parses your source first and asks AI for help second. Maturity: Active. See Data Import Wizard. Vocabulary grounding — link your environment's vocabulary to external authorities such as Wikidata and PeriodO. Maturity: Active. Limit: only the tenant administrator role can confirm a grounding. See Vocabulary Grounding. AI-assisted vocabulary bootstrap — a one-pass onboarding workflow that proposes an initial vocabulary set for your review, so the platform speaks your domain's language sooner. Maturity: Built. Limit: the proposal review screen is not yet available, so the workflow cannot be run end-to-end today; until it ships, vocabulary entries are authored directly on the live vocabulary surface. See AI-Assisted Bootstrap. Efficiency tips — short contextual nudges shown to researchers in the import wizard and workspace; switch them on or off per environment and review aggregate acceptance numbers. Maturity: Active. Limit: tips never block a researcher's action; aggregate numbers are only reported when enough activity exists to keep individual researchers unidentifiable. See Efficiency Tips. Citation integrity — structural guarantees behind citable editions and stable artifact versions. Maturity: Active. Limit: the platform does not mint DOIs itself; it exposes the stable identity an external DOI minter relies on. See Citation Integrity. Media review surface — a single page to review everything the platform extracted from one version of a media artifact, with manual additions, a re-extraction dry run, and promotion to a citable edition. Maturity: Active. Limit: promoting an edition requires the administrator role. See Media Review Surface. Entry Surface readiness — a review panel for your public search and browsing controls before you launch them. Maturity: Active. Limit: a review surface, not an auto-apply surface; making a control public is a separate, explicit step. See Entry Surface Readiness. Telemetry and privacy posture — what the platform records, what it does not, where the data lives, how long it is kept, and the data-protection rights it supports. Maturity: Active. Limit: capture is off by default; enabling it is an explicit, recorded decision. See Telemetry. Standards and citations — what the platform's standards support gives your environment without configuration, what you can configure on top, and what exports produce. Maturity: Built. Limit: some export profiles are still maturing; the standards overview carries per-item maturity. See Standards and Citations and the standards overview. User and access management — an older overview of the standard roles; the Permissions Panel is the live source of truth. Maturity: Built (legacy summary). Limit: role composition and custom-role authoring live in the Permissions Panel. See User and Access Management.

The most common administrator paths: Onboarding a new environment: configure voice and vocabulary by authoring entries directly on the vocabulary surface; confirm a few groundings if external authorities apply to your domain; compose permission roles and invite contributors; choose your citation style and have your platform operator apply it — a dedicated configuration screen is not yet available (see Standards and Citations); decide whether efficiency tips are on. Bringing in new source data: open the import projects list in the administration interface at /admin/data_import/mappingproject/ and use the upload button for your source type (Excel, MySQL, CSV bundle, or Coda). The wizard parses the source, classifies risk, generates proposals, and routes each proposal through a two-step review: a scholar approves it, then an administrator applies it. Reviewing media attestations: open the media record in the administration interface and follow its media-review link. Approve, amend, or strip per row; promote to an edition when the version is ready to cite. Auditing recent activity: open the Permissions Panel at /admin/permissions/ and use the Audit tab. Permission changes, ownership transfers, vocabulary edits, and reviewed AI-assisted changes all appear there. Checking what the platform is recording: /admin/monitoring/telemetry/ shows your environment's telemetry summary — which signals are being captured and in what volume.

Platform operations — tenant lifecycle, deployment configuration, incident response, and backups are handled outside your environment. For anything in that category, contact your platform operator.

A new environment opens with the platform's standard wording: the labels that title records in the workspace, and the confirmation phrases researchers approve before high-impact operations. Researchers are not blocked while that wording is still generic — the platform adapts its standard phrasing using the labels from your environment's own configuration. The AI-assisted bootstrap shortens the path to wording that speaks your researchers' domain language. It generates a starter set of wording proposals tuned to the research discipline your environment declares and its concept families (the kinds of records your environment defines), for you to review — accept, reject, or edit — in one pass during onboarding. Bootstrap is a one-pass onboarding tool. After onboarding, Voice and Vocabulary describes how your environment's wording resolves and the paths for shaping it. Note the availability limit below: the in-product screen for reviewing bootstrap proposals is not yet available, so the workflow cannot be run end-to-end today.

Proposal generation — Maturity: Built. Generates a starter list of suggested wording entries from your declared research discipline and concept families: suggested titles for records of each concept family, plus suggested phrasings for the four confirmation prompts researchers approve before high-impact operations (reorganising entries into a connected structure, permanently removing duplicate entries, updating the same identifier across already-saved entries, and applying a batch of structural changes as one step). Each proposal carries the suggested wording, a short explanation of why it is proposed, and a confidence score. Proposals come from built-in rules today; model-generated proposals are not yet available. All-or-nothing commit — Maturity: Built. Accepted proposals are written to your environment's vocabulary in a single transaction. If any write fails, nothing is written; you can resolve the cause and retry without partial results to clean up. AI-reviewed status with provenance — Maturity: Built. Every committed entry is recorded with AI-reviewed status and carries a tamper-evident cryptographic reference back to the proposal that produced it, so an entry's bootstrap origin stays provable. An explicit wording override for the same phrase takes precedence — explicit wording always wins over AI-reviewed wording. Proposal review screen — Maturity: Deferred. The screen where you accept, reject, or edit each proposal is not yet available in the environment admin interface. Until it ships, your environment's wording is shaped through the paths described in Voice and Vocabulary — naming your concept families, renaming roles, and asking your platform operator about a specific phrase.

Because the proposal review screen is not yet available: Name your concept families well — the highest-leverage wording move available today. The platform substitutes those labels into its standard phrases automatically, so a good set of names improves many phrases at once. See Voice and Vocabulary for where to set them and for the other wording paths. Rely on the standard wording in the meantime: record titles and confirmation prompts render from the platform's standard templates, adapted with your environment's own labels where available. An incomplete vocabulary does not block your researchers. Review the vocabulary arriving in your data through Vocabulary Grounding — a separate surface for the values found in your imported records, not for the platform's wording.

If you expected bootstrap to be enabled for your environment, contact your platform operator. When a researcher in your environment ratifies a binding set on a media artifact — saying "these terms correctly describe these regions of this artifact" — and a DOI is minted on top of that ratified state, the platform guarantees the cited data cannot silently change. A re-extraction run against a citable Edition is refused outright: it stops before any binding is touched. False-positive bindings a reviewer rejects stay rejected across re-runs. Read this when evaluating the platform for a peer-reviewed publication or a DOI-minted scholarly artifact, or when answering an institution's editorial, DPO, or library question about how citation integrity is enforced. This page explains the guarantees in plain language. The actions that produce the ratified state live on the Media Review Surface.

Three-layer artifact identity — every cited artifact carries three kinds of identity: a citable identity (the publishable artifact name plus an optional DOI, Zotero, or institutional handle); platform-internal identifiers that are never published; and the artifact's own natural self-description as the locator — glTF node names for 3D models, IIIF region selectors for images, TEI xml:id values for texts · Maturity: Active · Limit: the platform never rewrites the artifact file at ingest; internal identifiers stay internal. Working versions and citable Editions — every binding set belongs to an artifact version that is either a Revision (a working copy that can still change) or an Edition (frozen, citable, peer-review-targetable) · Maturity: Active · Limit: an environment may carry many Revisions of the same artifact; promoting one to an Edition is a deliberate, separate action. Explicit promotion to Edition — promoting a Revision to an Edition is a single confirmed action on the Media Review Surface; once promoted, the version is protected against re-extraction · Maturity: Active · Limit: requires the admin role. Edition freeze against re-extraction — the platform refuses any ingest run that would change the bindings of an Edition; the run stops with an error before any binding is touched · Maturity: Active · Limit: structural — not a warning, not a log entry. Durable rejection (Strip) — when a reviewer strips a false-positive binding, the platform keeps the record as a tombstone — a retained marker of the rejection — instead of deleting it, so later re-extraction recognises the rejection and refuses to re-propose the same binding · Maturity: Active. Reviewer-edit preservation in working versions — bindings a reviewer has approved or amended are marked as reviewer-owned; re-extraction never overwrites them, even while the version is still a Revision · Maturity: Active · Limit: bindings no reviewer has touched remain refreshable in a Revision. Per-action attribution — every review action records who acted, what the action was, when, and an optional note; this record is stored with the binding and is never deleted or rewritten by re-processing · Maturity: Active · Limit: the trail lives on each binding record; the platform does not keep a separate consolidated audit log of these review actions.

The guarantees described here are produced by actions on the Media Review Surface; this page describes what those actions mean for citation. Promote a citation-ready Revision to an Edition: open the Media Review Surface for the artifact, confirm the bindings are correct, and choose Promote to Edition (requires the admin role). Provide the Edition label, an optional DOI, and optional notes; a confirmation step precedes the promotion. Mint a DOI against an Edition: the platform does not mint DOIs itself. It exposes the Edition's stable identity — the artifact's public identifier plus its Edition label — so an external minter (your institutional library, a repository system, or a Crossref or DataCite membership) can target it. Strip a false-positive binding durably: on the Media Review Surface, choose Strip on the wrong binding and confirm. The rejection is permanent across re-extractions: future runs recognise it and do not re-propose the binding. Update the artifact file under an active citation: ask your platform operator to ingest the updated file under a new version label. The original Edition's data — and any DOI minted on it — stay intact; the new Revision is reviewed on its own merits and can be promoted to a new Edition later. The platform does not: Mint DOIs. DOI minting belongs to your institution's library or repository system; the platform provides the stable target. Host published papers. The platform holds the cited data, not the publication. Count citations. How often a published Edition is cited is a question for your institution's bibliometric tools. Embargo by date. There is no embargo or paywall workflow. If you need an embargo, hold the promotion to Edition until you are ready to publish, then promote.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A re-ingest of an artifact file was refused with a message that the version "is frozen for citation" The artifact version is an Edition; the platform refused to change it This is the guarantee working as designed. Ask your platform operator to ingest the file under a new version label; the original Edition stays intact. A reviewer stripped a binding last week, but the latest re-extraction proposed it again This should not happen — a stripped binding is preserved as a rejection across re-runs Contact your platform operator, identifying the artifact and the affected binding. Durable rejection is a structural guarantee; a recurrence is a platform defect. Promote to Edition is missing or disabled The artifact has not been ingested with a version yet, or your role lacks admin Confirm the artifact has been ingested (ingest creates the first version); verify your role assignment in the Permissions Panel. You need to embargo an Edition until publication The platform does not implement embargo workflows Keep the version a Revision in a private workflow until the embargo lifts, then promote. The platform does not restrict access to Editions by date. An audit reviewer asks for a formal audit log separate from the per-binding attribution Per-binding attribution is durable but lives on each binding record The per-binding attribution records — who acted, what the action was, when, and any note — are the audit trail, and re-processing never deletes or rewrites them. The platform does not keep a separate consolidated log of binding review actions; if the reviewer needs the records gathered into one export, contact your platform operator.

Tenant admin companions: Media Review Surface — the operational surface that produces the ratified state these guarantees protect; Telemetry — what operational signals the platform records and the privacy controls around them; Standards and Citations — what your environment inherits without configuration. The Data Import Wizard brings source data into your environment without bypassing review. It reads an uploaded source (an Excel workbook, a MySQL dump or live connection, a set of CSV files, or a Coda document), proposes how each table and column should land in your environment, routes every proposal through a two-step approval, and writes records only after you start the final import. Read this when you bring in a new corpus, re-import a source whose shape you already know, or a researcher reports that an import did the wrong thing. The wizard is the supported path for getting data into an environment. For repair work or bulk operations outside the wizard, contact your platform operator.

Ordered roughly by what you touch first. Guided entry from the sidebar — Imports & AI → Imports opens the first wizard step with your recent imports and saved setups. All imports lists every import, with shortcut buttons (Start import, Excel, Database, CSV files, Coda) in its top-right toolbar. Pending Review is a flat queue of suggestions awaiting review across imports. Background Jobs shows the status of background uploads. Maturity: Active. Limit: the plain admin "Add" form does not read a source — always start from an upload route. Excel upload — a project name, an optional description, and an .xlsx file. Files up to 5 MB import inline; larger files, up to 100 MB, run in the background. Maturity: Active. MySQL upload — two modes: a dump file (.sql or .sql.gz; 50 MB inline, up to 500 MB in the background) or a live connection address with optional credentials. Live-connection reads always run inline, and the credentials are held only for that request — they are never saved. A saved connection can reference a secret kept in the platform's managed secret store instead of carrying a password; the secret is resolved at run time. Maturity: Active. CSV upload — several files in one submission; each file becomes a table named after the file. Limits: 10 MB per file and 30 MB total inline; 50 MB per file and 250 MB total in the background. The wizard can suggest connections between files by matching overlapping values; these suggestions are deliberately more cautious than connections declared inside a single workbook. Maturity: Active. Coda upload — a project name, the Coda document name, a one-time API key, and an optional subset of tables. The key is kept only in your server session for that request and is never saved with the import. Maturity: Active. Background imports — an upload that exceeds its inline limit is refused before processing, with a message telling you the limit. Resubmit with the background option: a status page refreshes while the job runs and links to the wizard when it is ready. You can close the tab; the job keeps working. Maturity: Active. Six-step review flow — Step 1 Bring in your data, Step 2 Here's what we found, Step 3 What we'll do, Step 4 A few things to confirm, Step 5 Practice run, Step 6 Ready when you are. Nothing is written to your environment until you press Start import in Step 6. Maturity: Active. Autonomy setting (Step 3) — "How involved do you want to be?": Hands off, Stay informed, Ask if unsure, or Confirm everything, saved per import. The setting controls how many of the wizard's confident structural readings are applied for you — always with an undo window — versus held for your decision. At the two most hands-off settings this can include a change to an existing setup that has no imported records yet; at Ask if unsure, only additive changes the wizard is highly confident about move ahead; Confirm everything holds every suggestion for you. High-risk suggestions and restructure suggestions wait for explicit review whatever the setting. Maturity: Active. Suggestion cards with reasons (Step 3) — each card shows what would change, a confidence percentage, the evidence behind the reading, and plain-language reasons. Respond with Looks good or open Change this. Card actions are protected form submissions; a stray link click cannot alter a suggestion. Maturity: Active. Change a table's meaning — when the wizard read a table's meaning wrong, pick the correct meaning under Change this. The suggestion retargets cleanly: risk is re-assessed against the new meaning, and every card, preview, and the final import follow the correction. A card carrying an older unapplied change request shows a "requested, not applied yet" banner with Apply change and Keep original actions, and a plain confirmation cannot approve a stale meaning. Maturity: Active. Limit: a completed import is closed — to reinterpret its tables, start a new import. Undo for automatic decisions — when the wizard applies a suggestion for you, a toast names exactly what was decided, and "applied for you" always names its cause. The undo window pauses while you hover or focus the toast, and the paused time genuinely extends the window. When a setting change applies several suggestions at once, you get one combined toast with Undo all. Maturity: Active. Limit: undo reverses review decisions before the final import; it does not undo records written in Step 6. Confirmations that are remembered (Step 4) — your answers to the wizard's clarifying questions are saved with the import. Where retained source rows are available, a "show me" view displays the surrounding source cells so you can answer from evidence rather than memory. Later imports of the same shape reuse your answers. Maturity: Active. Practice run (Step 5) — a full dry run before anything is saved. Issues are grouped by cause rather than by row, with a good/warning/error breakdown, and each group links back to the review queue or exports a summary of the affected rows. Maturity: Active. Draft reader preview — an admin-only preview of how approved rows will read on your public entry surface, rendered by the same machinery the real import uses. Restructured fields are marked in the preview, including "keep both" companion fields. The preview publishes nothing. Maturity: Active. Saved setups and format recognition — a successful import creates or updates a saved setup. When you upload a familiar shape again, Step 2 shows "We've seen this format before" with a confidence figure, and every choice stays editable. Saved setups store structure, never your source rows. Maturity: Active. Decisions carried forward on re-import — when you re-import over already-imported data, decisions that are structurally unchanged from your prior import are carried forward instead of re-asked. Anything new, changed, or ambiguous goes back to review; uncertainty always routes to review, never to a silent carry-over. Maturity: Active. Two-step approval with risk levels — every suggestion gets a risk level (low, medium, or high) with visible reasons. A suggestion held for review goes through two steps: a reviewer approves first, then an administrator applies. When your autonomy setting lets a confident structural reading move ahead for you, both steps are recorded automatically with the setting named as the cause, and the undo window applies. Suggestions refined by AI always go through human review; AI never changes your environment directly. If the risk level changed while a suggestion sat in review — because the environment changed around it — apply is blocked until you read and acknowledge the new level. Maturity: Active. Needs revision — a reviewer can send a suggestion back with a required note instead of rejecting it outright. The suggestion blocks the final import until it is revised, and the note travels with it. Maturity: Active. Restructure suggestions — the wizard can propose shape improvements it detects in your source: a lookup column becomes a picker field, a supporting table becomes the option list behind a picker, or sibling language columns merge into one multilingual field. You choose Keep both (the original field plus a typed companion field) or Replace. Approved restructures are carried through the final import. These suggestions never apply automatically, whatever their confidence. Maturity: Active. Honest progress and receipts — the final run reports per-table progress as tables complete, with an explicitly approximate beat for the linking pass. The completion receipt leads with what happened: record and connection counts, "references not linked yet" with a per-link breakdown, and an Open your workspace action. Every table in the plan produces exactly one outcome row — "created N records", or "will create 0 records" with the reason — predicted in the practice run and confirmed after the run. An approved table can no longer produce nothing silently. Maturity: Active. Import assistant chat — a chat control on each wizard step that knows where you are in the flow. It can explain what it sees and propose actions, but a proposed action is never executed until you confirm it. Each import session has a chat budget; when the budget runs out the chat pauses and every import control keeps working. Your environment's AI settings can turn the assistant off. Maturity: Active. AI refinement is optional — when no AI provider is configured for your platform, the wizard still works end to end: the structural reading produces the suggestions, and the import is marked that AI refinement was unavailable. To enable AI refinement, contact your platform operator. Maturity: Active. Efficiency tips (Step 3) — short tip cards can appear alongside suggestion cards when tips are enabled for your environment. Tips never block an action. See Efficiency Tips. Maturity: Active. Import telemetry — when capture is enabled, import steps emit operational counts that carry no source content: no rows, filenames, document or table names, credentials, or tokens. See Telemetry. Maturity: Active. Limit: collection runs in the platform; a dedicated screen for browsing these metrics is not yet available.

Start in the sidebar at Imports & AI → Imports. Step 1 shows the source choices, your recent imports, and your saved setups. The All imports list offers the same upload routes as toolbar buttons. Submit the source that matches your shape — Excel, database, CSV files, or Coda. Within the inline size limit, the wizard reads the source immediately and opens the review. Above it, choose the background option and follow the status page; it links to the wizard when the job completes. Walk the six steps. Review what was found (Step 2), decide on suggestions and set how involved you want to be (Step 3), answer the clarifying questions (Step 4), and read the practice run (Step 5). Approve in two steps. A reviewer approves each suggestion, then an administrator applies it. If the risk level shifted while the suggestion waited, read the new level and acknowledge it before applying. Start the import (Step 6). Once every suggestion is approved or rejected, Start import becomes available. If your source needs a credential to read rows at import time — a Coda key or a live database password — Step 6 asks for it again and uses it only for that request. Watch the per-table progress, read the receipt, and use Open your workspace to see the results. If a run is interrupted, your setup, approvals, and practice run are kept; starting again resumes from the stopped table, and completed tables are not written twice. Risk levels in plain terms: Level What it means What happens Low The change is additive — a new table meaning, a new field, or no change to anything that exists. Quick lane. Confident low-risk suggestions can move ahead for you, with undo, depending on your autonomy setting. Medium The change alters an existing setup that has no imported records yet. Held for review by default. At the two most hands-off autonomy settings, a confident structural reading at this level can also move ahead for you, with undo. High The change alters a setup that already has imported records, or removes or merges whole tables. Held for explicit confirmation even after reviewer approval. Never applied automatically. A second pair of eyes is expected.

Re-importing a source you have brought in before is a normal operation: The wizard recognizes the saved setup, carries your unchanged decisions forward, and asks only about what is new or changed. For refreshing the records themselves, the platform supports two behaviours. Edit-preserving refresh matches incoming rows to existing records by their source identity, refreshes the values the source manages, and keeps researcher edits to fields the source does not manage — the right default for routine re-runs. Full refresh wipes the existing rows and reloads from scratch — destructive to researcher edits, only for genuine start-over situations. If you are unsure which behaviour a planned re-import will use, check with your platform operator before running it.

To enable AI refinement, contact your platform operator. For researchers: Adding and editing rows — what researchers see once imported data lands in the workspace. Environment admin companions: Voice and Vocabulary — the wizard's on-screen wording follows your environment's voice settings; Efficiency Tips — the Step 3 tip cards; Permissions Panel — who can review and who can apply; Telemetry — what import telemetry captures.

Tips are short, contextual suggestions the platform shows researchers while they work — in the review step of the import wizard and in the workspace — pointing out a faster way to do what they are already doing, or a field worth filling in. Tips are advisory: they never change data and never block anyone. As environment administrator, you decide whether tips appear in your environment at all, and the names tips use for your record types and fields come from your environment's vocabulary. Read this page when deciding whether to leave tips on at onboarding, when a researcher reports an unwanted or oddly worded suggestion, or when a kind of tip stops appearing.

Environment-wide tips switch — one setting turns tips on or off for your whole environment. It is on by default for new environments; off means no tips appear anywhere, regardless of any other setting. Maturity: Active. Tips during import review — when a researcher makes the same correction repeatedly while reviewing an import, a tip suggests fixing the underlying rule once instead of correcting the remaining rows by hand. Tip cards appear beside the correction cards in the review step. Maturity: Active. Tips in the workspace — when a selected record has noticeably fewer filled fields than similar records in your environment, a tip names a field worth adding. Maturity: Active. Confidence-tiered display — the most confident suggestions appear directly beside the researcher's work; middling ones wait under a collapsed "More suggestions" heading; anything below the confidence bar is not shown at all. Maturity: Active. Wording through your vocabulary — tip sentences are written by the platform, and the names they use for your record types and fields resolve through your environment's vocabulary. You adjust those names through vocabulary entries; you do not edit tip text directly. Maturity: Active. Per-family acceptance figures — the platform keeps aggregate figures per kind of tip — how often that kind was shown and how researchers responded — for your environment only, over a rolling 30-day window. Individual researcher actions are not reported. Maturity: Built; a self-service view of these figures is not yet available — contact your platform operator if you need them. Automatic quiet-down — a kind of tip your researchers consistently pass over can pause itself in your environment. The pause requires sustained low uptake (around four weeks) and a minimum number of researcher responses, so a quiet week does not silence a useful tip. Your platform operator is notified when a kind of tip pauses. Maturity: Built. Separate measurement switch — whether tip activity is measured is a separate per-environment setting from whether tips display, so tips can be shown without their activity being measured. When tips are off, nothing is shown, so there is no tip activity to measure. Measurement records which tips appeared and how researchers responded, without recording who. Maturity: Built. See Telemetry for what your environment records.

Decide at onboarding: tips are on by default for a new environment. Review how tips will read to your researchers — the record-type and field names come from your vocabulary (see Voice and Vocabulary) — and either leave tips on or have them switched off until your vocabulary is ready. Turn tips off for your environment: the environment-wide setting lives on your environment's platform record — contact your platform operator to change it. Once tips are off, no new tips are served anywhere; anything already on a researcher's screen clears the next time the page or wizard step loads. Change how a tip is worded: adjust the matching vocabulary entry, and the new name appears the next time the tip is shown. If the problem is in the sentence around the names rather than the names themselves, contact your platform operator. When a kind of tip goes quiet: this may be the automatic quiet-down. Re-enabling a quieted kind of tip is not self-service — contact your platform operator.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Researchers see no tips even though tips are switched on No tip pattern currently applies — tips fire only after repeated same-shape corrections during import review, or when a record clearly lags similar records — or a kind of tip has been quieted Tips are deliberately conservative; silence usually means no pattern was found. If a kind of tip that used to appear has stopped, contact your platform operator to confirm whether it was quieted. The import review step shows no tips panel Nothing cleared the confidence bar for that session Nothing to fix — low-confidence suggestions are held back by design, and the panel does not render when there is nothing to show. A researcher reports an unwanted or oddly worded suggestion The tip draws your record-type and field names from your environment's vocabulary, and the entry it found reads poorly in context Adjust the matching vocabulary entry — see Voice and Vocabulary. If the wording problem is in the surrounding sentence, contact your platform operator. A kind of tip stopped appearing after weeks of normal use It may have paused automatically because researchers consistently passed it over Contact your platform operator to review and re-enable it. Consider whether different vocabulary wording would help it land better.

Researcher tier: Tips and guidance — what researchers see and how tips behave for them. Tenant admin companions: Voice and Vocabulary — controls the names tip wording draws on; Data Import Wizard — the review step is the main place tips appear; Telemetry — what your environment measures and records. For platform-side questions — switching tips or tip measurement on or off, re-enabling a quieted kind of tip, requesting your environment's acceptance figures, or anything affecting other environments — contact your platform operator.

Before your environment exposes a public Entry surface — the published layer external readers will see — the readiness panel lets you review the filter ("facet") and autocomplete controls that would become public, record a decision about each one, and confirm or defer each candidate. Read this when preparing for a public launch, when a readiness report flags a compact-control warning, or when activating an additional public role. The panel is a review surface, not an apply surface. Recording a decision stores review state for your environment; promoting a public control or confirming your environment's search configuration is a separate, explicit step performed with your platform operator.

Readiness report — for every active public Entry role in your environment, the report lists the reviewed filter and autocomplete fields, candidate fields, compact-control warnings, blockers, and all stored decisions, along with how many records were sampled to produce it. Maturity: Active. Viewing the report requires admin access in your environment. Durable review decisions — each decision is stored with its action, your reason (required, up to 500 characters), your username, the time, and a snapshot of the evidence the report showed you. Maturity: Active. A decision is a review checkpoint; it does not change the public surface itself. Fixed decision actions — review candidate before promotion; choose shorter public label; defer candidate with reason; defer public control with reason; acknowledge long-value exclusion. The action list is fixed; the reason is free text. Maturity: Active. Environment isolation — the report and your decisions are always scoped to the environment you are signed in to. You cannot read another environment's report or record decisions for it. Maturity: Active. Refreshed report on every decision — recording a decision returns the updated report, including the newly stored decision, and confirms that your environment's search configuration was untouched. Maturity: Active.

Sign in to your environment's admin area at /app/admin/ with an account that has admin access. The Entry Surface readiness panel sits in the side column, next to the source-data refresh panel, and loads the current report as the page opens. The refresh button at the top of the panel re-runs the report at any time. The summary line shows the overall status — "Ready for scalar probe" once at least one public role has reviewed single-value filter fields, "Needs review" otherwise — along with the number of roles, warnings, and recorded decisions, and a "ratification unchanged" indicator confirming that review work never alters your environment's search configuration. Review compact-control warnings. The report flags fields where some values are too long to show in a compact public filter control. Each flagged field appears with a reason box and the actions that are valid for it; the panel shows up to three fields per role at a time. A field you have decided on stays in the list, now showing its stored decision with the action and reason you recorded. Record a deferral. When a candidate should not become public yet, defer it with a reason. The deferral is durable: the next report shows the stored decision, and the field stays deferred until you record a different decision. Walk the pre-launch checklist. Each role section lists its blockers, reviewed fields, candidates, and recorded decisions. Work through them row by row; every decision requires a reason. Hand off for launch. When the report reads clean and your environment is ready, your platform operator performs the public launch. Recording decisions is the review checkpoint that precedes the launch — it is not the launch itself. If the server rejects a decision — a missing reason, or an action that is not valid for that field — the panel shows the server's message inline.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The panel reports that readiness is unavailable, or you land on the sign-in page Your account does not have admin access in this environment Ask an existing environment administrator to grant admin access, or run the review from an admin account. Recording a decision fails with a validation message The reason is missing, or the chosen action is not valid for that field Read the message in the panel. Add a reason, or choose one of the actions the panel offers for that field. The panel reports no active public Entry roles Your environment does not have a public Entry role configured yet Public Entry roles are set up as part of preparing your environment for launch. Contact your platform operator. The report reads clean but the public Entry surface has not appeared Recording decisions does not promote public controls or launch the surface Confirm with your platform operator that the launch step was run. The panel is a review surface only. The "ratification unchanged" indicator worried you This is by design — recording decisions never changes your environment's search configuration Confirming the search configuration is a separate explicit operation performed with your platform operator. The indicator exists so you can verify nothing changed as a side effect of your review. You need to undo a recorded decision Decisions are durable review state Record a new decision for the same field. It replaces the earlier one; the report then shows the latest decision with its reason and time.
Public reader — what researchers and external readers see once your public Entry surface launches.

The media review surface is a single page where you review every attestation tied to one version of a media artifact, add attestations the automatic extractor missed, dry-run a re-extraction before applying it, and promote a working revision to a citable Edition. Read this when reviewing a freshly ingested media artifact, when the extractor proposes bindings that look wrong, or when you are ready to promote a revision to an Edition so a DOI can be minted against it. Two terms the page uses throughout: an anchor is an addressable point inside the artifact (for a 3D model, a named node in the model file), and an attestation is the recorded link between an anchor and a term in your environment. The guarantees described in Citation Integrity rest on the review decisions you take here.

Attestation summary card — anchor count, attestation count, mapped / unmapped / overridden / auto / orphan-anchor tiles, and the last-extracted timestamp. Maturity: Active. Counts are scoped to the artifact version the page resolved. Per-row Approve / Strip / Amend actions — one row per attestation; every action is recorded with your name and a timestamp. Maturity: Active. Strip is a recorded rejection, not a deletion: the decision is kept so a later re-extraction cannot silently re-propose the same binding. Manual attestation add — record a binding the extractor missed. A typeahead searches the term records in your environment as you type; you can also paste a term record's id directly, and optionally attach an anchor id and a note. Maturity: Active. The typeahead depends on search being activated for your environment; the paste path works regardless. Re-extraction dry run and apply — re-run the extractor against the same artifact, first as a dry run that reports what would change without writing anything, then as an apply. The job runs in the background and the panel polls its status. Maturity: Active. The panel reports overall job status only — queued, running, succeeded, or failed — not step-by-step progress. Requires the Admin role. Edition promotion — promote a working revision to a citable Edition, with a required Edition label and optional DOI and notes. Maturity: Active. Requires the Admin role. Once promoted, the Edition is frozen: the platform refuses any re-extraction against it. Reviewer-decision preservation — approvals, amendments, strips, and manual additions are all marked as reviewer decisions and survive re-extractions; the extractor never silently overwrites them. Maturity: Active.

The page is reachable two ways: Direct URL: /admin/epistemic/epistemicentity/<id>/media-review/, where <id> is the media record's id. The page opens only for media records. Deep link from the record: open a media record in the admin; below the record's form, a banner labeled "Media review" links to "Review attestations for this artifact"; click through. Access requires signing in to the admin; signed-out visitors are redirected to the sign-in page. Review actions and manual additions require the Editor or Admin role in your environment; re-extraction and Edition promotion require Admin. The common review paths: Approve a correct binding: select Approve on the row. The decision is recorded with your name and timestamp, and future re-extractions leave the binding alone. Strip a wrong binding: select Strip and confirm. Your rejection is recorded, and the extractor's next run will not re-propose the same binding. Amend with a note: select Amend, write the note, save. The binding stays in place; your note and the reviewer-decision mark are preserved across re-extractions. Add a missing attestation: open the manual-add dialog and start typing the term; select a match from the suggestions, or paste the term record's id. Optionally attach an anchor id and a note, then save. The new row is marked as a manual reviewer addition. Dry-run a re-extraction: expand the "Re-run extractor (advanced)" section and select Dry run. The job runs in the background and the panel polls its status until it succeeds or fails. Compare the dry-run report against the current state before you apply. Apply asks for confirmation, because it writes new anchors and attestations. Promote to Edition: select Promote to Edition, enter the Edition label, and optionally a DOI and notes. A confirmation step precedes the promotion. After promotion the Edition is frozen — further extraction work requires a new working revision. The summary counts refresh automatically after each action, so the tiles always reflect the decisions you have taken so far.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The page errors on load The media record is missing required data fields Check the browser console for messages beginning media_review: — the page reports exactly which field is missing. Confirm the media record carries the required fields. Add the source-file link to the record. The rest of the page still works for reviewing existing attestations. The typeahead returns no matches for a term you know exists Search has not been activated for your environment, or the search found nothing for your query The picker shows a hint when this happens; paste the term record's id directly — the dialog works regardless of search state. To get search activated for your environment, contact your platform operator. If the button is still missing, contact your platform operator. A re-extraction job stays "running" for a long time Large artifacts can take time to process Wait — the status will move to succeeded or failed. The panel reports overall status only, not step-by-step progress. You stripped a binding but the next extraction proposed it again This should not happen — a strip is durable across re-extractions Contact your platform operator with the artifact id and the details of the stripped binding.
