The Permissions Panel at /admin/permissions/ is the single surface for who-can-do-what in your environment. Contributor roles, custom role composition, project safety rules, wording overrides, ownership hand-off, and the project-history lookup all live here. Read this when changing a contributor's role, composing a custom role, handing off project ownership, or answering "who reviewed that import, and when?".

Contributors tab — every contributor in your environment, with their assigned role and last activity. Change a contributor's role, adjust individual permissions, or narrow the scope of their assignment. Maturity: Active. Limit: the panel manages roles and permissions for existing contributors; contributor accounts are created by your platform operator — see User and Access Management. Roles tab with custom role composition — the standard roles come preloaded; custom roles are composed from a fixed set of permission building blocks. A standard role can be renamed inline; the new name is a display label only. Maturity: Active. Limit: the building blocks themselves are fixed by the platform. Role scoping — a role assignment (or a custom role) can be limited to specific record types or fields. Maturity: Active. Limit: a scope only narrows where the role applies; it cannot add permissions the role does not grant. Project rules tab — set your environment-wide review policy: whether high-impact saves need a reviewer who did not author the change, and how destructive changes are confirmed — by two contributors, or by a single contributor through an elevated confirmation step. Maturity: Active. Limit: the panel saves and displays these choices as your environment's declared policy; how each applied change was actually confirmed, and by whom, is shown on the Project history tab. Review learning setting — on the Project rules tab: opt in to record privacy-safe signals from your team's review decisions so future suggestions improve. Maturity: Active. Limit: off by default; switching it on requires acknowledging the privacy notice, and the change is recorded along with which admin made it. Wording tab — rename the permission-related labels shown in your environment, starting with role names. Maturity: Active. Limit: changes compose with your environment's voice and vocabulary settings; there is no separate translation table to maintain. Vocabulary review prompt — when the panel loads, it checks permission-related wording and flags entries that need review, with the reason and a link to edit each one. Maturity: Active. Limit: the check is read-only — it never changes anything; you act on a finding or dismiss it. Project history tab — look up the recorded history of an applied import proposal: its status, how it was confirmed, who reviewed it and when, the recorded reason, and the permissions that were in force at the moment it was applied. A record carries an "Edited after apply" marker when the applied content was changed afterwards. Maturity: Active. Limit: lookup is per proposal — you supply the proposal's ID from the import screens; records are read-only. Ownership hand-off — the current project owner can hand ownership to another contributor. The hand-off asks for explicit confirmation for both sides, completes as a single change, and is recorded. Maturity: Active. Limit: only the current owner can start a hand-off, and the new owner must be an active contributor holding the administrator role with permission management. Display density control — switch the panel between compact, cozy, and comfortable layouts. Maturity: Active. Limit: cosmetic only — it affects rendering, not permissions; the choice is remembered in the browser where you set it.

The panel's address is /admin/permissions/. It opens on the Contributors tab; the other tabs are Roles, Project rules, Wording, and Project history. The active tab is kept in the page address, so a bookmark or a shared link opens the panel on that tab. Change a contributor's role: Contributors tab, open the contributor's row, pick the role. To limit where the role applies, set a scope on the same row. Compose a custom role: Roles tab, combine the permission building blocks, name the role. Rename any role's display label inline with the edit control; the underlying building blocks stay fixed. Set project rules: Project rules tab. Switch the separate-reviewer requirement on or off, choose the destructive-change policy, and save. Enable review learning: Project rules tab. Switch the setting on, acknowledge the privacy notice, and save. The decision is recorded along with who made it. Hand off ownership: as the current project owner, use the "Hand off ownership" control, choose the new owner, and confirm for both sides. Look up an import's history: Project history tab, enter the proposal's ID, and load the history. The record shows the review decision and the permission snapshot from the moment of apply. Review flagged wording: when the vocabulary check finds entries needing review, a notice appears. Open the Wording tab, follow each flagged entry's edit link, or dismiss the finding.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A notice says permission wording needs review The load-time vocabulary check flagged entries Open the Wording tab. The check is read-only; follow the edit link on each flagged entry, or dismiss the finding. See Voice and Vocabulary. Renaming a standard role did not change what it allows A rename sets a display label only; the role's permission building blocks are fixed This is the intended behavior. Compose a custom role if you need a different set of building blocks. A contributor cannot act on content their role should allow Their role assignment carries a scope that excludes that content Open the contributor's row and check the scope. Widen it or remove it. The ownership hand-off will not complete Only the current owner can hand off, and the new owner must be an active contributor holding the administrator role with permission management Give the intended new owner the administrator role with permission management first, then run the hand-off again. Review learning is on, but suggestions do not seem to improve Signals accumulate gradually and stay within your environment This is expected early on. The setting records your team's review decisions over time; it does not change behavior immediately.

Companion pages: Voice and Vocabulary — the wording system the panel's overrides plug into; User and Access Management — the standard role set and how contributor accounts are created; Telemetry — what the review-learning setting records. Platform-level operations — cross-environment concerns such as incident response and platform-wide data-protection records are handled outside this panel. Contact your platform operator.

This page is the environment administrator's working view of the platform's standards support. It tells you which standards-backed capabilities your environment inherits without configuring anything, what you can configure on top, what published entries expose to the outside world, and what stays your environment's own interpretation. Read this when an institutional reviewer asks "what standards does our knowledge environment comply with?", when a federation partner asks whether a specific export format is supported, or when you are deciding which standards a field in your environment should declare conformance with. The cross-audience overview is the Standards & Compliance Overview; this page is for someone running an environment.

These capabilities ship with every environment. None of them require per-environment engineering, custom code, or a separate contract. Each carries a maturity tag; the standards overview records the audited maturity of every standard the platform engages with. Stable, citable identity for published artifacts — a published artifact carries a stable public identity that an external identifier service (your library's DOI minter, for example) can target. The platform does not mint DOIs itself, and data cited against a frozen Edition cannot silently change · Maturity: Active · See Citation Integrity for the guarantees in detail. Citation framework built on Citation Style Language (CSL) — citations render through CSL styles, the same open format reference managers and journals use. A catalog of more than seventy standard styles ships with the platform (Chicago and APA among them), and each environment holds its own active styles · Maturity: Built · Limit: a style that is not in the catalog can be installed on request — contact your platform operator. Per-entry citation export in CSL JSON — every published entry's citation is available in CSL JSON, the interchange format reference managers read · Maturity: Built. Media locators that follow IIIF and W3C Web Annotation conventions — a cited region of an image, audio/video segment, or 3D model is addressed by the artifact's own natural self-description (an image region selector, a 3D-model node name, a text passage identifier), never a platform-invented code · Maturity: Built · Limit: locator support ships today; dedicated standard viewers are not yet integrated. See Citation Integrity. Vocabulary review backed by shared authorities — vocabulary values first seen in your imported data queue for review rather than being guessed at, and AI suggestions (when enabled) can reference public authority records: Wikidata for entities and concepts, PeriodO for historical periods. Suggestions are advisory only — a reviewer declares or rejects every value · Maturity: Active (the review queue); the authority-backed AI suggestions are Built · See Vocabulary Grounding. Typed, self-describing API — integrations read published data through a documented GraphQL API: a typed contract a partner can inspect, not an undocumented internal surface · Maturity: Built. Privacy-aware telemetry — activity records are redacted before they are stored and kept in a tamper-evident chain, supporting a defensible data-protection posture under GDPR · Maturity: Active · See Telemetry. Accessibility controls in the reading interface — readers can adjust font size, line height, color presets, and font family. The platform targets WCAG 2.2 AA; a full audit against that target has not yet been recorded · Maturity: Active. Capability-to-standard quick reference: Capability Backing standard(s) Stable citable identity for published artifacts DOI (minted externally against platform-held identity) Deep-linkable image / AV / 3D regions IIIF, W3C Web Annotation Citations consumed by reference managers CSL Vocabulary review informed by shared authorities Wikidata, PeriodO Typed API for integrations GraphQL Accessible reading interface WCAG 2.2 AA (target) Defensible data-protection posture GDPR

Citation style — per environment and per entry type. Adopt a style from the shipped catalog, or refine one through the review workflow described below. Applying a style requires the administrator role; styles are versioned, and the platform refreshes published citations after a style is applied · Maturity: Active. Vocabulary grounding — declare or reject queued vocabulary values through the Vocabulary Grounding workflow, with a display label of your choosing and optional links to standards from the platform's recognized list · Maturity: Active. Field standards declarations — a field definition in your environment can declare which standards its content conforms to, chosen from the platform's approved standards list. Declarations are validated when you save the field definition — a standard outside the list is rejected with a validation message — and the declarations are visible through the API · Maturity: Active. Voice and vocabulary substitution — independent of standards but composes with them: your wording is yours, the structural conformance underneath is the platform's. See Voice and Vocabulary · Maturity: Active. Reference evidence and citation rules — declared once per published entry type; described in the next section · Maturity: Active. How often you touch each of these: Citation style — once at environment setup; revisit when you adopt a new venue's or institution's style guide. Vocabulary grounding — during onboarding, and after any import that brings in vocabulary values your environment has not seen before. Field standards declarations — when designing or revising a field definition. They are part of the field's definition, not a day-to-day switch. Voice substitution — whenever the platform's default wording feels foreign to your researchers. Reference evidence and citation rules — once per published entry type, when deciding how its References section should read.
documents.s: What you can configure on top

documents.t: When a published entry shows a References section — one row per piece of evidence, each with a scholarly citation — two declarations on the entry type produce it. Both are configuration, not code: the platform supplies the machinery, your environment supplies the meaning. The evidence declaration — where your evidence lives and how it joins. You declare which record type holds the occurrences of an entry (the passages, witnesses, specimens, or find records), which link connects them to the entry, and which of your columns carry the locators (page, chapter, line, quote) and the source details (author, work, editor). Every column name in the declaration is your environment's vocabulary; the platform never assumes any of it. Citation rules — how citations are built and styled. You declare which of your columns map to the standard citation fields (author, title, editor, date, page), and which CSL style renders them. The result is a formatted citation per evidence row, plus standalone source citations beneath the evidence list. Two behaviors worth knowing when designing the declarations: Editions are optional. An occurrence with no published edition — a researcher's own catalogued manuscript or fragment — still appears as a full evidence row. Evidence is never gated on the existence of a published edition. Paired-edition bridging. When an occurrence is catalogued against more than one edition — say a modern critical edition and an early printed one — the row bridges them in the classics convention: the modern citation first, then = volume.page (abbreviated editor) for the paired edition. The abbreviations and locators are your data; the bridge composition is the platform's. Citation appearance (punctuation, abbreviated author forms, locale) is managed through CSL styles, not by editing rendered text. If a citation looks rough, the fix is a style refinement — see the review workflow below and the troubleshooting table.
documents.s: Reference evidence and citations on published entries

documents.t: When your environment publishes entries, the outside world can rely on: A rendered citation on each published entry, produced against your active CSL style · Maturity: Built. The same citation in CSL JSON at a stable address per entry, ready for import into reference managers · Maturity: Built. Typed API access through which an integration partner reads published data under the same visibility rules as the reading interface · Maturity: Built. Machine-readable semantic export formats — JSON-LD representations of published entries and research-object packaging for archival hand-off — are committed in the platform's architecture but not yet available. The standards overview records the current maturity of each format; point a federation partner there rather than promising a format ahead of its maturity tag. Exports are produced by the platform; your environment does not build or maintain a custom export pipeline. What is yours is the data, the wording, and the entry-type design — not the export machinery.

The day-to-day operator paths: Pick a citation style at environment setup: the platform's citation-style service lets you browse the shipped catalog and adopt a style per entry type. A dedicated configuration screen is not yet available — the service is operated through the platform's administrative citation endpoints, and your platform operator can run the selection with you. A style that is not in the catalog can be installed on request. Declare a field's standards conformance: edit the field definition and choose from the platform's approved standards list. A declaration outside the list is rejected with a validation message when you save. Review new vocabulary values: work the review queue through the Vocabulary Grounding workflow. When AI suggestions are enabled, a suggestion can reference a matching Wikidata or PeriodO record to inform your decision. Answer "what standards does our knowledge environment comply with?": point the asker to the standards overview. It is written for exactly that conversation, and its maturity tags distinguish what ships today from what is committed but still on the way.

When the active style renders roughly for your material, a style is refined through a three-step review path, so no one person silently changes how every citation reads: Propose. A proposed style (or a refinement of the active one) is generated from sample citations you want to match. The proposal is measured against your environment's pinned citation test cases and assigned a risk class (low / medium / high) based on how many existing citations it would change. Scholar review. A scholar reviews the proposed style, its differences from the active style, and its risk class before approving. Admin apply. Once scholar-approved, an administrator applies it. The style is stored in your environment — no code change is involved — and the platform refreshes published citations after the style is applied. Styles are versioned and never auto-applied by the platform; AI assistance never changes a published citation directly. The workflow runs through the platform's administrative citation endpoints today; a dedicated review screen is not yet available. Your platform operator can walk the three steps with you.
documents.s: Refining a citation style (the review workflow)

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix A published entry shows no References section The entry type has no evidence declaration — the platform does not guess where evidence lives Declare it on the entry type: the occurrence record type, the connecting link, and the locator and source columns. Evidence rows appear but without formatted citations No citation rules declared for the entry type, or the chosen citation style was not found Add citation rules mapping your columns to the standard citation fields, and confirm the style name matches an installed style exactly. Citations render with awkward punctuation or separators The active CSL style has not been refined for your material Refine the style through the review workflow (scholar reviews, admin applies). Do not hand-edit rendered text — the next refresh would overwrite it. An internal reference code appears inside a rendered row A locator or source-detail declaration points at a linking column rather than a plain-text column Re-point the declaration at the human-readable column; linking columns belong only in the join declaration. A style your researchers need is not pre-loaded CSL is an open standard; the style file is portable XML Contact your platform operator to install it. Provide the CSL file or a published style URL. A standards declaration is rejected when you save a field definition The declared standard is not on the platform's approved list Choose a standard from the list, or ask your platform operator to evaluate adding the one you need. The list is deliberately narrow: every entry on it is one the platform can stand behind. A vocabulary value cannot be declared or rejected from the review queue The acting account lacks the review permission for grounding decisions Ask an environment administrator to take the decision, or to grant your role the review permission — see Permissions Panel. A federation partner needs a machine-readable export format Semantic export formats are committed but not yet available Point the partner at the maturity tags in the standards overview, and raise the need with your platform operator. Neither you nor the partner should have to take a conformance claim on faith.

Cross-audience parent: Standards & Compliance Overview. Tenant admin companions: Citation Integrity — the published-citation guarantees in detail; Vocabulary Grounding — the Wikidata / PeriodO workflow; Voice and Vocabulary — your wording on platform surfaces; Telemetry — what the platform records and how it is protected.

The platform collects a deliberately small set of operational signals about how it runs — never a copy of your research content. This page tells you what those signals are, where they live, how long they are kept, what you control, and what to tell an institutional DPO or IRB. Read it when onboarding under a Data Processing Agreement, when an institution's information-security team asks the standard onboarding questions, or before enabling any optional capture. The default posture is capture-off: AI-call, import-run, and review-decision capture record nothing until switched on for your environment. The one exception is tip-activity capture, which starts on — with its own off switch — so that unhelpful tip categories can pause automatically.

AI-call records — for each AI call the platform makes on your environment's behalf, a structured record: the task, the model and its version, token counts, latency, a refusal or escalation flag, and the verdict of a prompt-injection screening check. The record carries one-way hashes of the prompt and response — never the raw text. A call whose prompt matches a high-risk personal-data pattern (such as an identification number) is dropped entirely: no record, no hash, no count. Maturity: Active. Import-run records — for each import run: the source format, entity counts before and after, error categories (never error values), and duration. By construction these records contain no personal data: raw source rows, filenames, staged file paths, document and table names, and credential references are deliberately not recorded. Maturity: Active. Review-decision records — structured signals from suggestion review: reject, undo, edit-after-apply, and feedback-button events, each with a structured reason code. The record carries a keyed fingerprint of the suggestion's shape, not its content, and never records free-form reviewer comments. Maturity: Active. Tip-activity records — which efficiency tips surfaced and whether they were accepted, aggregated into acceptance ratios that drive the automatic pausing of unhelpful tip categories. Tip records carry no researcher identity at all — which tip appeared and what happened to it, never who. Automatic pausing acts on a tip category only once it has at least five recorded responses (the default minimum sample), so it never reacts to a single researcher's actions. Supports the Efficiency Tips surface. Maturity: Active. Search-quality records — planned aggregate measures of search health (zero-result rates, hashed query patterns with small-count suppression). This signal class is not capturing yet: today the platform stores no search-query telemetry at all, raw or hashed. Maturity: Deferred. Per-environment capture switches — capture is controlled per signal class for each environment, and every switch starts off except the tip-activity pair, which starts on. Enabling review-decision capture additionally requires a recorded privacy acknowledgment (who acknowledged, when, and which version of the privacy notice) before the switch will take effect. Maturity: Active. Environment telemetry panel — a dashboard showing your environment's own signals: counts per signal class, a suggestion-quality summary, and any automatically paused suggestion categories. It reads only your environment's records and never displays raw source rows, filenames, file paths, credentials, or tokens. Maturity: Active. Telemetry export for access requests — a self-service, audit-grade export of your environment's telemetry is planned but not yet available. Today, your platform operator produces the export for you on request. Maturity: Deferred.

Read what is happening in your environment: open /admin/monitoring/telemetry/. The panel shows your environment's signal counts by class, the suggestion-quality summary, and any paused automatic-suggestion categories. It is scoped to your environment only; cross-environment comparisons exist only on the platform operator's side. Turn capture on or off: capture switches live on your environment's platform record and are changed through the platform's administrative console — contact your platform operator to change your capture posture. Each signal class is switched independently; everything except tip-activity capture starts off. Enable review-decision capture: this switch requires a privacy acknowledgment to be recorded first. The acknowledgment (person, timestamp, notice version) is stored with your environment's record and is enforced — the switch cannot be turned on without it. Control efficiency-tip capture: tip surfacing and tip-event capture each have their own switch on your environment's record. Both are currently on by default. Tip-event capture continues while both switches are on, even where other capture classes are off — this keeps the automatic pausing of unhelpful tips working. See Efficiency Tips. Honor a data-access request (GDPR Article 15): contact your platform operator, who produces a telemetry export scoped to your environment. Honor an erasure request (GDPR Article 17): see the right-by-right table below; route the request through your platform operator. The configurable settings, summarized: Setting What it does Default Per-signal capture switches Turn each telemetry class (AI calls, import runs, review decisions) on or off for your environment. Changed by your platform operator. Off Review-decision privacy acknowledgment Required before review-decision capture can be enabled; records who acknowledged, when, and which notice version. Not acknowledged Tip surfacing Whether efficiency tips appear at all in your environment. On Tip-event capture Whether tip surface/acceptance events are recorded, independently of other capture classes. On Minimum sample for automatic tip pausing The number of recorded tip responses a category needs before automatic pausing will act on it, so the mechanism never reacts to a single researcher's actions. Changing it is a platform-level change — ask your platform operator. 5

Each environment's data lives in its own separate compartment of the database — its own database schema. The database itself enforces that isolation, and telemetry honors it: telemetry tables refuse to be read from outside an environment's schema. Data Where it lives Who can read it AI-call records (structure and hashes) Your environment's schema You; platform team (read-only, for support) Import-run records Your environment's schema You; platform team (read-only) Review-decision records Your environment's schema You; platform team (read-only) Tip-activity records Your environment's schema You; platform team (read-only) Cross-environment operational metrics (cost, latency, model name) Platform-level storage; never your content Platform team only Cross-environment metric rows identify an environment by an internal identifier and carry model name, token counts, cost, and latency — never content.

The platform's default retention policy per data class: Data Default retention AI-call records (structured shape) 30 days verbatim, then 12 months as hashed aggregate Import-run records 12 months Validation and abuse audit records (security-relevant) 2 years (GDPR Art. 17(3)(e) — defence of legal claims) Confirmed prompt-injection material (quarantined) 90 days; extendable under legal hold for specific incidents These defaults are calibrated against ICO and EDPB operational-log guidance, ISO/IEC 27001:2022 control A.8.15, and EU AI Act logging requirements. For retention questions beyond this table — including shorter environment-specific retention — contact your platform operator.

Right How the platform handles it Access (Art. 15) Your platform operator produces a telemetry export scoped to your environment, with an accompanying manifest. Rectification (Art. 16) Not applicable to operational telemetry. For environment content, rectification flows through the standard editing surfaces. Erasure (Art. 17) User-identifying telemetry rows are pseudonymized in place. Small-count-suppressed aggregates are retained as anonymous data (Art. 17(3)(d)). Restriction (Art. 18) Verbatim capture for a specific person can be suppressed on request while anonymous aggregates continue. Portability (Art. 20) Same export format as Article 15. Object (Art. 21) Per-person suppression on request; an environment-level objection turns the signal class off entirely. Automated decision-making (Art. 22) The platform does not make automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects on data subjects. AI output is advisory; researcher review gates any change to your data. Lawful basis is Legitimate Interest (Art. 6(1)(f)), with a documented assessment per signal class available from your platform operator. A data-protection impact assessment precedes production capture and is refreshed annually; environment-specific documentation is available on request.

Third party What they see AI model vendor Under the platform's standard routing, AI calls run inside a cloud provider's hosted model service, and the model vendor does not receive your data. Confirm the routing in force for your environment with your platform operator. Cloud provider hosting the model service Runs the model on each call; provider-side invocation logging is kept off, so the provider retains only the call envelope (model, role, timing) — not prompts or responses. Platform team Read-only access to your environment's schema for support; access to platform-level operational metrics (cost, latency — never your content). Anyone else Nothing. No third-party analytics, advertising, or telemetry services.

When an environment offboards, its database schema is dropped — all telemetry payload in it is deleted, including every aggregate stored there. Cross-environment operational metrics (cost and latency at the platform level) are retained for cost-history continuity; they identify the environment only by an internal identifier and contain no content. On request, that metric trail can be deleted too; the trade-off is the loss of platform-level cost-trend history for the periods your environment participated in.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The telemetry panel shows no signals Capture is off — the default for every signal class except tip activity. Search-quality telemetry is not capturing yet for anyone. Ask your platform operator to enable the signal classes you need. Review-decision capture also requires the privacy acknowledgment to be recorded first. An import run reports that a stored service credential could not be retrieved The stored credential for that import source is missing, expired, or unreachable Check the import source's connection settings, or contact your platform operator. The telemetry row records the outcome only — no credential material is ever in a telemetry record. A DPO asks for the legitimate-interest assessment per signal class The assessment is maintained per signal class as platform documentation Contact your platform operator, who supplies the documented assessment for the signal classes in question. A researcher exercises the right to be forgotten Handling depends on the data class User-identifying telemetry rows are pseudonymized in place; anonymous aggregates are retained as anonymous data. Route the request through your platform operator. You want to verify no raw search queries are stored Raw query text is not captured at all in the current platform — the search-quality signal class is not yet capturing in any form Nothing to configure. When search-quality telemetry ships, it will store hashed, small-count-suppressed aggregates, not raw queries.

For researchers: Privacy and safety. Environment admin companions: Permissions Panel — the Project history tab records who reviewed what, and when; Efficiency Tips — the tip-capture switches. For platform-level monitoring, data-protection impact assessment records, or residency requirements, contact your platform operator.

When your records bring in vocabulary the platform does not already recognize — today, calendar names appearing in your data and standard identifiers declared on your field definitions — the platform collects each new value in a review queue instead of guessing what it means. Grounding is that review step: you decide, value by value, whether each one becomes a recognized part of your environment's vocabulary, with a label of your choosing and optional links to recognized scholarly and data standards. Read this when you are working through the review queue after an import, when you want AI help proposing matches against public reference sources, or when a researcher reports that a vocabulary value was reviewed incorrectly.

Vocabulary review queue — every watched vocabulary value first seen in your data appears in a review list, with its category, how often it occurs, and its review status (shown as Ungrounded, Tenant-declared, Promoted, or Rejected). Maturity: Active. Limit: the platform currently watches two categories — calendar names in your records and standard identifiers on your field definitions; queue rows are created by the platform from your data, and you cannot add rows by hand. Declare a value — accept a value into your environment's vocabulary, with an optional display label (leave it blank to use the value itself) and optional links to standards from the platform's recognized list (TEI, CIDOC-CRM, IIIF, CSL, and others). Maturity: Active. Limit: within one vocabulary category, two declared values cannot share the same label. Reject a value — mark a value as not belonging to your vocabulary, with an optional reason kept for the audit record. Maturity: Active. AI grounding suggestions — when enabled for your environment, the platform can propose a grounding for a queued value: a suggested label, suggested standards, and — where a match exists — a reference to a public authority record. Wikidata supplies candidates for entities and concepts; PeriodO supplies candidates for historical periods, including each period's time range and regional coverage as the authority describes them. Maturity: Built. Limit: suggestions cover common reference-data categories only (calendars, standards, place types, period types, media kinds, languages, scripts); there is not yet a button in the review queue for requesting one — suggestions are requested through the platform's administrative API, and the review queue shows a notice when suggestions are available but not yet switched on for your environment. Privacy screening for external lookups — before any value is sent to an external reference source, the platform classifies it. Only values that are clearly public reference data are looked up externally; values that resemble personal or private data are never sent outside your environment. Maturity: Active. Limit: the screen is deliberately cautious — a blocked lookup costs you a manual check, never a data leak. Decision capture on AI suggestions — each decision you take on an AI suggestion (accepted as-is, edited before applying, rejected) is recorded as a structured signal for audit and quality measurement. Maturity: Active. Limit: these records stay within your environment. AI usage controls — AI suggestions are switched off by default for each environment, and usage is capped by a rolling token budget. When the budget runs out, suggestions pause and manual review continues unaffected. Maturity: Active. Limit: the budget has a platform-defined maximum. AI availability notice — a fixed, platform-written notice on the review queue tells you when AI suggestions are available but switched off for your environment. Administrators who manage permissions see a link to the settings page; other reviewers see guidance to ask their administrator. Maturity: Active. Limit: the wording is platform-controlled and cannot be customized.

The review queue lives in your environment's admin interface, alongside the other vocabulary surfaces. Work the queue after an import: open the ungrounded vocabulary list. Filter by category or by review status to focus on what is new. Each row shows the value, its category, and how many times it occurs in your data. Declare one or more values: select the rows, choose the declare action, and confirm on the follow-up page. You can set a shared label (or leave it blank so each value becomes its own label) and pick any standards the values comply with from the provided list. Declared values stop appearing as unreviewed in future imports. Reject values that do not belong: select the rows, choose the reject action, and optionally record a reason on the follow-up page. The reason is kept with the audit record. Turn AI suggestions on: AI suggestions are off until enabled for your environment. When the feature is available, the notice at the top of the review queue links administrators with permission-management access to the settings page; see Permissions Panel. Enabling AI suggestions and adjusting the token budget are administrator-only actions; if you do not find these controls on the settings page, contact your platform operator. Trust re-imports: re-importing your data never resets a review decision. A value you have already declared or rejected keeps its status; the platform only updates how often it occurs. Every grounding decision — declare or reject, manual or AI-assisted — is written to the platform audit log with the acting administrator, the value, and the outcome.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The declare action refuses your label Another declared value in the same vocabulary category already uses that label (capitalization does not matter) Choose a different label, or leave the label blank so each value is labeled as itself. A standard you want to link is not offered in the list The standards list is platform-managed; only recognized standards can be attached Declare the value with the standards available now. To request an addition to the list, contact your platform operator. An AI suggestion arrives without an external reference, or marked as reduced confidence The privacy screen blocked the external lookup, or the public source returned no match — the suggestion was produced from the value alone The suggestion is still usable. Review it manually before accepting, or reject it and declare the value yourself. AI suggestions stop arriving partway through a session Your environment's rolling token budget is used up, or AI suggestions were switched off — either in your environment's settings or platform-wide Manual review keeps working. Check your environment's AI settings; if the feature is unavailable platform-wide, contact your platform operator. A value you already reviewed shows as unreviewed after a re-import This should not happen — re-imports never reset review decisions Contact your platform operator with the affected value and the import date. You want to change the wording of the AI availability notice The notice is platform-controlled and cannot be edited per environment Share environment-specific guidance with your reviewers through your own channels rather than working around the notice.

Voice and Vocabulary — configuring the wording your researchers see across the platform. AI-Assisted Bootstrap — the one-pass onboarding path that can run alongside grounding review. Standards overview — which scholarly and data standards the platform recognizes and what each enables.

The platform talks to your researchers constantly — page headers, button labels, confirmation phrases, tips, chat copy. Voice and vocabulary is how you make that text speak your environment's language instead of generic platform English. Read this when onboarding a new environment, when a researcher asks "why does it say X?", or when a platform phrase needs to use your wording. Wording configuration is an environment-admin concern; researchers see the result but do not edit it. It applies only to text the platform itself emits — researcher-authored content is never reworded.

Per-environment wording entries — every platform-emitted phrase resolves through a wording table scoped to your environment, one entry per phrase. Surface families displayed today: import wizard pages, workspace headers and toolbar labels, assistant chat copy, permission and role wording, and telemetry panel labels. Maturity: Active. Limit: an entry only takes effect where the platform actually asks for that phrase. Built-in baseline with your labels substituted — every environment starts with a complete neutral-English baseline, and the platform automatically substitutes the names you gave your concept families (the categories your records belong to — "Person", "Place", "Text") into those phrases. A fresh environment already speaks in its own category names before anyone writes a wording entry. Maturity: Active. Layered resolution — for each phrase, the platform uses the most specific wording available: an explicit override set for your environment, then an AI suggestion you accepted during onboarding, then wording seeded during setup, then the baseline. Maturity: Active. Visible failure instead of blank text — if a phrase has no entry and no baseline, the platform renders the phrase's internal dotted key (for example wizard.stage3.match_card.header) rather than showing nothing. A raw key on screen is a signal, not your configuration error. Maturity: Active. Permission wording overrides — role names and permission labels can be renamed from the Permissions Panel. Renaming changes the displayed wording only, never what the role can do. Maturity: Active. AI suggestion provenance — a wording entry that came from an accepted AI suggestion carries a tamper-evident reference to the suggestion it came from. Maturity: Active. Limit: tamper-evident, not hidden — it proves origin, it does not encrypt anything. Two further families prepared, not yet displayed — the wording table also holds confirmation phrases for high-impact actions and review-history labels. Both are seeded with baseline wording, but no screen displays either family yet, so entries for them have no visible effect today. Having or lacking your own phrasing for these never blocks an action or locks any part of onboarding. Maturity: Built.

The highest-leverage move is naming your concept families well. Most of what researchers read is the baseline with those names substituted in, so a good set of category labels improves hundreds of phrases at once. Name your concept families: set the display label for each category of record your environment manages. This normally happens while you confirm an import; the labels can also be edited afterwards in your environment's admin area. Every platform phrase that mentions the category updates. Rename roles and permission wording: open the Permissions Panel and edit the role's displayed name inline. The underlying permissions are unchanged. Accept AI wording suggestions at onboarding: see AI-Assisted Bootstrap for the assisted onboarding path that proposes environment-specific phrasings for you to accept or reject. Act on the wording review notice: the Permissions Panel shows a read-only review notice when concept-family labels are missing or look machine-generated. Fix the flagged labels; the notice can also be dismissed, but it returns if your labels change again. Override a specific phrase: there is currently no self-service screen for editing an individual wording entry. If a specific platform phrase needs different wording and the paths above do not cover it, contact your platform operator.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A platform phrase shows generic wording in your environment No environment-specific wording exists for that phrase, so the baseline is rendering Check that the concept family the phrase mentions has a display label — that fixes most generic-sounding phrases. For a specific phrase that still needs different wording, contact your platform operator. A page shows a raw dotted key like wizard.stage3.match_card.header instead of readable text The phrase has no wording entry and no baseline — the platform deliberately shows the key so the gap is visible This indicates a platform-side gap, not an error in your configuration. Contact your platform operator. The wording review notice in the Permissions Panel returns after you dismissed it Dismissal applies to the labels as they were; the notice reappears when your labels change Fix the flagged labels rather than re-dismissing. The notice is read-only and never changes anything itself. You renamed a role but its permissions did not change Renaming a role changes its displayed wording only This is the intended behaviour. To change what a role can do, compose a custom role in the Permissions Panel.

Researcher tier: Workspace walkthrough — what researchers see (your wording in action). Tenant admin companions: AI-Assisted Bootstrap — assisted onboarding wording suggestions; Vocabulary Grounding — a different surface: grounding the research vocabulary in your data against external authorities; Permissions Panel — role renaming and the wording review notice.

This page covers team membership and the standard role set. It is the lightweight overview; the live source of truth for contributors, roles, project rules, ownership transfers, and project history is the Permissions Panel. Read this if you want a one-page summary of the role model; go to the Permissions Panel page when you are about to make a change.

Standard role catalog — four pre-loaded roles every environment ships with: Reviewer, External collaborator, Researcher contributor, and Project admin. Maturity: Built. Limit: the permissions behind a standard role are fixed by the platform; renaming a standard role changes its label only. Custom role composition — build a role by combining permissions from the platform's fixed permission set. Maturity: Active. Limit: you combine existing permissions; you cannot define new ones. Project rules — environment-wide safety rules that sit on top of roles, such as requiring a second contributor to confirm high-impact changes. Maturity: Active. Limit: rules tighten what a role allows; they never grant more. Ownership transfer — moves ownership of the environment from the current owner to another contributor. Maturity: Active. Limit: only the current owner can start a transfer; both the owner and the receiving contributor must confirm; every transfer is recorded.

The Permissions Panel at /admin/permissions/ is where you do this day-to-day. The panel has five sections: Contributors, Roles, Project rules, Wording, and Project history. Role names follow your environment's wording settings, so the role names you see may differ from the standard names used on this page. Assign or change a role: Contributors section. Pick the contributor and choose a standard or custom role. A role assignment can also be limited to specific record types or fields. Compose a custom role: Roles section. Combine permissions from the platform's set and name the role. Roles can be renamed at any time; a rename changes the label your team sees, never the permissions. Set project rules: Project rules section — for example, require that high-impact changes are confirmed by a second contributor. Transfer ownership: available to the current owner only. The owner starts the transfer, both sides confirm, and the transfer is recorded. Add a new contributor: contributor accounts are created by your platform operator. Once the person appears in the Contributors section, you assign their role there. Standard role summary: Role What it allows Typical contributor Reviewer Read and review suggested changes; cannot save changes. External reviewers, students. External collaborator Review and save small additive changes in a focused area, without broader project authority. Guest collaborators from outside the project. Researcher contributor Review suggestions, save routine changes, undo recent changes, and manage saved import setups. Project team researchers. Project admin Everything, including high-impact changes, field setup, role management, and review metrics. Project directors, principal investigators.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A contributor cannot open the Permissions Panel Their account does not have administrator access Ask a contributor with the Project admin role to check their role in the Contributors section. If no one in your environment can resolve it, contact your platform operator. You need a permission shape no standard role provides The standard catalog is fixed Compose a custom role from the available permissions. If the permission you need does not exist in the platform's set at all, contact your platform operator. Renaming a standard role did not change what it allows Renaming changes the label only This is the intended behavior. Compose a custom role if you need a different set of permissions. A contributor can review changes but cannot save them Their role does not include saving (for example, Reviewer), or a project rule requires a second contributor for that kind of change Check the contributor's role in the Contributors section and the rules in the Project rules section. An ownership transfer will not complete Transfers must be started by the current owner; both sides must confirm; and the receiving contributor must be an active contributor holding the Project admin role with role management Confirm on both sides, and check the receiving contributor's role in the Contributors section. If the transfer was not started by the current owner, ask the owner to start it.
Live source of truth: Permissions Panel.

You are a scholar, student, archivist, or editor working in a knowledge environment built on this platform. You sign in, read, search, edit drafts, and cite records. You do not run the system; you use it. This guide is the entry point for everything researcher-facing. Read it when you join a new environment, when a control is not behaving as you expect, or when you want to know what the platform will and will not do for you. If you configure the environment — turning columns on or off, choosing which fields are searchable, managing other researchers' permissions — see the environment administration guide instead.

The researcher surface gives you eight capabilities, ordered by how often you will reach for them. Workspace table view — the main table of records for each record type, with a toolbar, a Manage columns panel, filters, a row-density toggle, and a Details panel for reading a full record. Maturity: Active. Limit: which controls appear for each record type is configured per environment; if a control you need is missing, your environment administrator can expose it. Inline editing and drafts — edit a field directly in the table: double-click a cell to open it and press Enter to save, while longer and multilingual fields open an editor with its own Save and Cancel buttons. + New row opens a drawer where your draft is saved as you work and becomes a full row when you choose Activate row. Maturity: Active. Limit: on a brand-new row, fields that link to other records become editable after the first save creates the draft. Search across scripts — a quick search finds records across the collections you can access, a full Search & Read page filters and reads results in place, and the toolbar box narrows the rows already in front of you. Search matches the scripts your records carry — original script, transliteration, and translation — for fields marked searchable. Maturity: Active. Limit: only fields your environment marks searchable are covered. Media and citations — records can carry images, audio, video, and 3D models, and each media item carries a citation in your project's citation style, ready to copy. Maturity: Active. Limit: which media a record carries depends on what your project attached. Public reader and draft preview — a stable read-only view of published records, with an in-workspace preview that shows a record as a reader outside the project would see it. Maturity: Active. Limit: which records reach the reader depends on your project's review and publish workflow. Tips and guidance — small suggestions that appear in the workspace and in multi-step wizards. You can dismiss a single tip or mute a whole family of tips. A tip only suggests; acting on it is always your choice. Maturity: Active. Accessibility — keyboard navigation, visible focus indicators, the row-density toggle, and controls for font size, line height, font family, and color presets. Maturity: Active. Limit: screen-reader announcement coverage continues to improve. Privacy — the platform records usage as aggregate counts and timings, not transcripts of what you typed, and masks sensitive text before anything is stored. Privacy and safety explains exactly what is recorded and what is not. Maturity: Active.

Start with whichever matches what you want to do. New to the workspace, or unsure where a control lives → Workspace walkthrough. Creating a new record, picking up an abandoned draft, or editing an existing record → Adding and editing rows. Hunting for a record across scripts, opening media, or reading citations → Searching and reading. Curious about the small suggestions appearing beside the form or the table → Tips and guidance. Driving the platform from the keyboard, or adjusting display settings → Accessibility. Wondering what the platform records about you and what it does not → Privacy and safety. Wanting to know what a reader outside the project sees, and how to preview it → Public reader. Stuck on one specific task, or after a quick answer in the moment → the in-product Help page (/app/workspace/help) groups short task-shaped guides by topic, and a ? beside a control opens the matching guide in a drawer. Browse the same guides in the help topics (see find help on a topic). A few conventions across all walkthroughs: Bold marks an on-screen control name — for example, + New row, Add filter, Activate row. A code-style font marks a path, URL fragment, or literal value. Examples use abstract content ("historical figures", "manuscript editions") rather than your specific project's records. The mechanics are the same regardless.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Where to escalate A column you expected is missing from the table. Either hidden in the current view, or not exposed in your environment's configuration. Open Manage columns in the toolbar; if the column is not listed there, ask your environment administrator to expose it. Your environment administrator. A field is read-only when you expected to edit it. Permissions on your account, or a workflow rule for that record type. Confirm your role with your environment administrator; if the restriction is intended, request edit permission for that record type. Your environment administrator. A draft will not activate. A required field is still empty. The drawer highlights the required fields that are still empty — fill them, then choose Activate row again. See Adding and editing rows. Your environment administrator, if the message is unclear. Search returns nothing for a record you know exists. The relevant field is not marked searchable in your environment's configuration. Open the record directly through its Details panel; ask your environment administrator to mark the field searchable. Your environment administrator.
Environment administration guide — the companion guide for the person who configures your environment. Help topics — the same short, task-shaped guides that the in-product Help page shows.

Your knowledge environment is built to work with keyboard navigation, screen readers, and adjustable display settings. This page walks through what is available, where to find it, and what is still on the way. Read it when you want to drive the workspace without a mouse, when you need to adjust how text is displayed, or when a control is not reachable or readable the way you expected.

Workspace keyboard navigation — Tab / Shift+Tab, Enter, Escape, arrow keys, and Space cover the workspace's interactive controls. The combinations follow common conventions. Active. Visible focus rings (keyboard-only) — a clear outline on the focused element, drawn when you navigate with the keyboard and suppressed for mouse clicks, so the screen stays quiet for mouse users. Active. Inline editing with the keyboard — Tab into a field, type, Tab out; your change is saved when the field loses focus. Enter saves it too. Dropdown fields respond to arrow keys and Enter. Active. Hints on fields that are not editable yet — a field whose editing surface has not shipped shows a hint in place of an editor. The hint is part of the keyboard tab order and is announced as disabled to screen readers, so you know the field exists and is intentionally not interactive yet. Active. Row density control — three row heights (Compact, Cozy, Comfortable); your choice is saved with the view you are working in. Active. Accessibility control panel — font size, line height, font family, and a small set of background color presets, remembered by your browser. Available on your environment's reading and browsing pages; the workspace does not include it yet. Active. Finer-grained color customization is Deferred. Accessible inline tips — the tip panel that appears alongside your work is screen-reader-friendly and keeps focus stable when its content updates. Active.

Tab / Shift+Tab moves through interactive controls — toolbar buttons, filter controls, the search box, table cells, drawer fields. Arrow keys move within the table grid, the saved-views menu, and the row density control. In the column manager, the arrow keys on a column's reorder handle move that column up or down the list. Space selects the focused row. Hold Ctrl (Cmd on Mac) with Space to add a row to the selection or remove it. Shift + Up/Down arrow extends the selection across a range of rows. Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on Mac) opens the focused row's details. Enter activates the focused button or saves an edit in a focused field. Escape closes the active drawer, panel, or dialog. Focused elements show a visible focus ring — a clear outline marking where you are. The ring is keyboard-only by default; clicking a control with the mouse does not draw it.
documents.s: Driving the workspace from the keyboard

documents.t: Tab into a field, type, then Tab out — your change is saved as soon as the field loses focus. Pressing Enter saves it too. For dropdown fields, arrow keys move through the options and Enter selects one. For related-record lookups, type to search, then Tab to a result and press Enter to link it. Escape closes the panel when you are done.

Some fields show a "not editable yet" hint instead of an editor. These hints are deliberately part of the keyboard tab order and are announced as disabled to your screen reader, so it is clear the field exists and is intentionally not yet interactive. They are not skipped, not invisible, and they do not pretend to be editable.
documents.s: Fields that are not editable yet

documents.t: The table toolbar has a row density control with three settings — Compact, Cozy, and Comfortable. Pick whichever works for your eyes and workflow; your choice is saved with the view you are working in, so it is there when you come back. On your environment's reading and browsing pages, the accessibility control panel adjusts how text is displayed. Open it from the accessibility button in the page header — announced to screen readers as "Open accessibility settings" — or press Alt+A. The panel is not available inside the workspace yet. It lets you adjust: Font size — make all text larger or smaller as a percentage of the base size. Line height — increase line spacing for easier reading; particularly helpful for dyslexia and low vision. Font family — switch between the default font and alternatives. Background color — a small set of page background presets, useful for contrast and reducing glare. A Reset to defaults button restores the standard settings. These settings are remembered by your browser on the device where you set them. If you sign in from a different device or browser, set them again there.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A control is not reachable with Tab. A gap in the focus order. Try Shift+Tab from a nearby control that is reachable. If the control still cannot be reached, contact your environment administrator — an unreachable control is a bug, not a setting. Your screen reader skips a "not editable yet" field. Your screen reader is set to skip disabled controls, or the hint did not load. Turn on your screen reader's setting for reading disabled controls. If the field is still skipped, contact your environment administrator. No focus ring appears after pressing Tab. You last interacted with the mouse — the ring is keyboard-only — or the page styling is interfering. Press Tab once more. If the ring still does not appear, contact your environment administrator. Font size resets after you sign out. Display settings are stored in your browser; the browser's stored data was cleared, or you are in a different browser or a private window. Re-apply the setting in the accessibility control panel. These settings do not follow your account across devices. You cannot find the accessibility control panel in the workspace. The panel lives on the reading and browsing pages; the workspace does not include it yet. Open a reading page and use the accessibility button in the page header, or press Alt+A there. Inside the workspace, use the row density control and your browser's own zoom. Your row density choice does not stick. The choice saves to the view you have open; the save may not have completed. Set the density again with the view open. If it still resets, contact your environment administrator. The highest-contrast preset is still not enough for your needs. The preset set is deliberately small for now; finer color customization is deferred. Use the preset closest to your needs and tell your environment administrator about the gap — reports shape what gets built next. An inline edit does not save when you Tab out. The field is read-only for your role, or the value failed validation (look for an inline error). Correct the value if there is an error shown. For a permissions question, contact your environment administrator.

Workspace keyboard navigation: Active. Visible focus rings: Active. Row density control: Active. Accessibility control panel on the reading and browsing pages (font size, line height, font family, background color presets): Active. Inline editing with the keyboard: Active. Discoverable hints on fields that are not editable yet: Active. Accessible inline tips: Active. Screen-reader announcement coverage — for example, a spoken confirmation when an edit saves — is still expanding.
documents.s: What is there, what is still arriving

documents.t: Accessibility problems are bugs, not configuration questions. If a control cannot be reached from the keyboard, a screen reader misreads a field, or poor contrast makes text unreadable, contact your environment administrator so the problem reaches the people who can fix it.
documents.s: If something is not working for you

This page covers creating new records and editing existing ones in your workspace. The model is: a new row is created as a draft the moment you ask for one, every edit saves as you finish each field, and your draft stays in the table until you complete it. There is no Save button to forget. Read this when you create your first record, when you want to know what "draft" means for a new row, or when an edit is not behaving as you expect.

Create a row from the toolbar — one click adds a draft row to the current table and opens it for editing. Active. Insert and duplicate — insert a row directly below an existing one, or duplicate a row to start a new one from its values. Active. Autosave editing — every change saves when you finish the field. There is no Save button. Active. Draft stage for new rows — a new row starts as a draft: visible to your project, never shown to public readers, and not yet linkable to other records. Active. Editing in two places — the table cells and the Details panel edit the same record; a change made in one shows in the other. Active. Linked-record fields — search the related record type and pick a match, directly inside the field. Active for records past the draft stage. Row deletion from the workspace — not yet available. Deferred.

Open the table you want to add to. New rows always belong to the table you are looking at. Click + New row in the toolbar. Your environment may label this button differently. The row is created right away as a draft: a notice confirms Draft row created, with a Review row button that takes you to it, and the row joins your table and opens for editing. Fill in the fields. Each field saves when you finish it — click out of a text field or press Enter, and the value is stored. Choices and checkboxes save the moment you pick them. Leave and return whenever you like. Your draft is a row in your table. Close the panel, navigate away, come back another day — your values are saved. Click the row to continue where you left off. Required fields can stay empty while you draft. They must be filled before the row can leave the draft stage. Two more ways to start a row: Insert row below — right-click an existing row and choose Insert row below. In views you order by hand, the new row lands directly below that one; in sorted or filtered views, the active sort and filters decide where it appears. Duplicate row — right-click a row and choose Duplicate row. This creates a new draft with that row's directly editable values copied in; derived and linked fields are skipped. If + New row is unavailable, the button itself tells you why. Some views cannot accept new rows — for example, a view that combines or filters records rather than showing a single stored table.

A new row begins as a draft: Your project sees it. Draft rows appear in the workspace table alongside everything else. Public readers never see it. Only records that have been completed and published reach the public reading site. It cannot be linked yet. The platform declines attempts to link a draft row to another record — the link is refused with a message rather than saved. Required fields may wait. A draft saves with required fields empty; the row cannot become an active record until every required field has a value. Once every required field is filled and the row passes its checks, it can leave the draft stage and become an active record — after that, links to other records save normally.

You can edit in two places, and they stay in step: In the table — edit a cell directly. The change saves when you confirm it or move on to another cell. In the Details panel — click a row to open its Details panel. Click into a field, change the value, then leave the field or press Enter. The panel header shows Saving… and then Saved. A value you did not change is not re-saved. Not every field takes typed input: Fields marked with a Read badge are not editable in place. These are derived fields (computed from other fields), media fields, and field types that do not have an in-place editor yet. To change a derived value, edit the fields it is computed from. Relation fields show the linked-records editor instead: existing links appear as removable chips, and a search box lets you type part of a related record's name and pick a match to add a link. Click the × on a chip to remove a link. If a save fails, an error message tells you what went wrong. The field returns to its stored value — re-enter your change after fixing the problem.
Removing rows from the workspace is not yet available — the row menu shows Delete row as unavailable. If you created a row by mistake or need a record removed, contact your environment administrator.

Symptom Likely cause Fix + New row is unavailable. No table is selected, or the current view cannot accept new rows. Hover over the button to see the reason, or switch to a regular table view. Creating or editing a row fails with a permission message. Your role includes read access but not edit access. Contact your environment administrator. A field will not accept your edit and shows a Read badge. The field is derived from other fields, holds media, or has no in-place editor yet. Edit the fields it is computed from. If you believe the field should be directly editable, contact your environment administrator. You cannot link another record from a new row. The row is still a draft. Records cannot be linked while either side is a draft. Fill in the required fields and complete the row first. If linking stays unavailable afterwards, contact your environment administrator. A change did not save. The value failed a check, or the field never lost focus. Look for an error message near the field or panel. Click outside the field or press Enter to confirm the save, then re-enter the value if it reverted. You need a row deleted. Row deletion from the workspace is not yet available. Contact your environment administrator. A field you expected is missing from the form. The field is hidden in the current view, or it is not configured for this record type. Check the view's hidden fields first. Otherwise, ask your environment administrator to add the field.

What you can do in the workspace reflects your role in the project. Members with read access browse, search, and view Details; adding and editing rows requires edit access. If your role does not include editing, the platform declines the change with a permission message. Roles are assigned by your environment administrator; the permissions panel page describes what each role covers.

When you add a row to a table, the platform creates it as a draft right away — no Save button needed. Every field you fill in saves the moment you leave it. Your draft is a real row in your table; you can close the panel and come back to it another day. When every required field is filled, the row can leave the draft stage and become an active record.

Open the table you want to add to. Click + New row in the toolbar. Your environment may label this button differently. A confirmation notice appears — Draft row created — and the row opens for editing. Fill in the fields. Each value saves when you click out of the field, press Enter, or make a choice. There is no Save button to forget. Leave and return whenever you like. Your values are stored. Click the row in the table to pick up where you left off. Required fields can stay empty while you draft. They must be filled before the row can be activated. Two more ways to start a row: Insert row below — right-click an existing row and choose Insert row below. Duplicate row — right-click a row and choose Duplicate row. The new draft starts with that row's editable values already filled in — a useful way to create a second entry that shares most of the same details. If + New row is unavailable, hover over it to see why. Some views cannot accept new rows — for example, a view that combines or filters records rather than showing a single stored table.

A new row begins as a draft: Your project sees it. Draft rows appear in the workspace table alongside every other row. Public readers never see it. Only records that have been activated and then published reach the public reading site. It cannot be linked yet. If you try to link a draft row to another record, the platform declines with a message. Finish the draft first. Required fields may wait. A draft saves even if required fields are empty. The row cannot be activated until every required field has a value.

Once you have filled in every required field and the row passes its checks, it can leave the draft stage and become an active record. After activation, the row is no longer a draft — it is a full record in your collection, and links to and from other records work normally. Activation is not the same as publication. An activated record is visible to your project but not yet public. A separate publish step sends it to the public reading site. See Preview an entry before publishing.

Symptom Likely cause Fix + New row is unavailable or greyed out. The current view cannot accept new rows. Hover over the button to see the reason, or switch to a regular table view. Creating a row fails with a permission message. Your role includes read access but not edit access. Contact your environment administrator. A field did not save after you typed a value. The field may not have lost focus, or the value failed a check. Click outside the field or press Enter. Look for an error message near the field, then re-enter the value if it reverted. You cannot link another record from a new row. The row is still a draft. Links to other records are not accepted until the row is activated. Fill in the required fields so the row can leave the draft stage, then try again. The row stays in the draft stage. One or more required fields are still empty. Look for a message near any empty field, fill in every required field, and try again. The row you added has disappeared from the table. It may have been filtered out of the current view. Remove or adjust any active filters, or switch to a view that shows all rows.

Alongside search, a published environment offers an index — a browsable, alphabetised list of every entry. It is the way to explore the whole corpus when you are not looking for one specific item.

A project can publish more than one index, and you switch between them from the controls at the top of the list. For a multilingual corpus that often means browsing the same entries by transliteration or by original script — the same entries, ordered and bucketed by whichever index you pick. The available indexes are chosen by your project; you see only the ones it publishes.
Each row in the index can show more than a bare headword — typically the transliterated form, the original-script form, and a short gloss together — so you can recognise an entry without opening it.

A character rail runs alongside the index. Click a letter to jump straight to that bucket; the list pages as you scroll, so even a very large corpus stays responsive. Which index is the default, and what each row shows, are set by your project when the environment is published — different projects will offer different index choices.
You do not need a spreadsheet or data file to start. You can create collections, define their fields, and wire up relations between them directly in the workspace — no import wizard required.
documents.s: Build a knowledge environment from scratch without importing

documents.t: A knowledge environment is made of: Collections — the types of things you are keeping track of (people, manuscripts, events, places — whatever is relevant to your project). Fields — the pieces of information you record for each item in a collection (a person's name, a manuscript's date, a place's region). Relations — links between collections that let you say "this person wrote this manuscript" or "this event happened in this place." All three are created the same way whether you are starting from scratch or refining a set that an import created.

Open the workspace. In the sidebar, look for Add collection (or New collection) in the collection list. Give the collection a name — for example, "People" or "Manuscripts". Choose the concept family that best describes the things in this collection (person, document, place, event, and so on). This helps the platform apply sensible defaults for search and display. Confirm. The empty collection appears in your sidebar. It has no fields yet; you add them next.

Open the collection. Click Field Definitions in the toolbar or sidebar. Click Add field. Give the field a label — the name as you want it to appear in the table (for example, "Full name", "Date of composition", "Language"). Choose the field type: text, number, date, select (a list of options), or other types your project supports. Optionally mark it Required (see Make a field required). Save. Repeat for as many fields as the collection needs. You can always add more fields later. When you create a field this way, the label you type is the only name it ever has. There is no source column name to fall back on — what you typed is exactly what appears everywhere.

A relation lets a record in one collection point to a record in another. For example, a field on "Manuscripts" that points to a "People" record for the author. Open the collection where the relation field will live (e.g., "Manuscripts"). Click Field Definitions → Add field. Give it a label (e.g., "Author"). Choose the field type Relation (or Link to collection). Select the collection this field points to (e.g., "People"). Save. When you open a Manuscripts record, the "Author" field shows a picker that lets you search and select a People record. The link is live — clicking the linked record opens that person.
documents.s: Creating a relation between two collections

documents.t: You can mix import and manual. Start with a skeleton you build by hand, then import data later. Or import first and add extra fields by hand. The rules are the same either way. Relations you create manually are immediately active. Unlike some imported relations that go through a review queue, manually created relations are ready to use as soon as you save. Your labels are your labels. Every field you create from scratch is researcher-owned from birth — no import will ever overwrite the label you gave it (see Rename a field label). Removing a field. If you later decide a field is not needed, you can remove it from Field Definitions. Existing records lose that field's value; it is not recoverable unless you restore the field.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Add collection is not visible in the sidebar. Your role may not have permission to create collections. Ask a project administrator. The concept family I need is not in the list. Only the concept families enabled for your project are listed. Ask an administrator to enable the one you need. A relation field I created is not showing the picker when I open a record. The relation may need a moment to become active, or the target collection has no records yet. Refresh the record; if the target collection is empty, add a record there first. I created a field but it does not appear in the table columns. New fields may not be visible in all views by default. Open the Column manager (from the toolbar) and enable the field.
