When you open a published entry — or its draft preview — the reading view shows the entry's citations rendered in your project's citation style. Select and copy the text to paste it into a bibliography, footnote, or document. Citations sit in the entry's References area. Rows of evidence carry their citations, and when your project has set up a citation for the record itself, it appears as its own row there too. Read the references section on a published entry explains what each row means.
documents.s: Copy a citation for a record or media item

documents.t: A media item attached to a record can carry its own citation details — separate from the record's citation. When your project has given a media item full citation details, its citation appears among the entry's references, rendered in your project's style and ready to copy.

Your project's citation style is set by your environment administrator. It is defined in Citation Style Language — the same format reference managers such as Zotero use. Different collections within your project can use different styles.
documents.s: What citation style your project uses

documents.t: The draft preview shows an entry exactly as a reader will see it, references and citations included, so you can copy a citation before anything goes live — see Preview an entry before publishing.
documents.s: Copying before an entry is public

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix A citation shows placeholder text or looks incomplete. The fields the citation draws on are missing or only partly filled in on that record or media item. Open the record in your workspace and complete those fields. The citation updates on the next publish; the draft preview shows the result first. If the needed fields are not clear, ask your environment administrator. The citation style looks wrong for your field. Your project has not yet declared a citation style for that collection, or the style is still being refined. Contact your environment administrator. Citation styles are set per collection; the citations update once a style is applied. A citation renders roughly — punctuation or ordering looks off. The collection's citation style is a proposed draft that has not yet been reviewed and applied. Raise it with your environment administrator. A reviewed and applied style replaces the rough rendering on the next publish. No citation appears for a media item. The media item's citation details are missing, or your project has not set up citations for media items in that collection. Complete the citation fields on the media item's record, or ask your environment administrator whether media citations are set up for that collection.

You can pick any number of rows in your table and either copy them to your clipboard (to paste into a spreadsheet) or download them as a file. A floating toolbar appears as soon as you select at least one row and disappears when you clear the selection.

One row: click any cell in the row. Add rows one at a time: hold Ctrl (Windows / Linux) or Cmd (Mac) and click each additional row. Select a range: click the first row, then hold Shift and click the last row. Every row between them is selected. The toolbar shows the count of selected rows and stays visible while you work.

With your rows selected, click Copy selected in the toolbar. The visible columns of those rows are placed on your clipboard, with a header row of column labels, and a message below the table confirms how many rows were copied. Switch to a spreadsheet, press Ctrl/Cmd+V, and the rows paste into cells, ready to use.

Click Export selected to download the selected rows as a JSON file — a structured data format. Your browser saves the file to your usual downloads location. If you want your rows in a spreadsheet, use Copy selected instead and paste them in.
Click the × at the right end of the toolbar — or, while the toolbar is focused, press Escape. The toolbar disappears and no rows remain selected.

The toolbar also shows Delete, Edit visibility, and Set row color. All three are visible but not yet available — they are waiting on a platform update. Clicking them does nothing. Selecting rows in one view does not carry over to another view or to another table. Switching views or tables clears the selection.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Clicking a row opens the record instead of selecting it. You may have clicked the row's Open details button rather than the row itself. Click the row's background, not the action buttons at its end. The toolbar does not appear after clicking a row. The click may have landed on a control — a button, the drag handle, the color strip — instead of a data cell. Or a cell editor is open. Click one of the row's data cells. If a cell editor is open, press Escape to close it first. A "Copy failed" message appears after clicking Copy selected. Your browser blocked clipboard access for this site. Allow clipboard access in your browser's site settings for this environment, then copy again. Delete, Edit visibility, or Set row color does nothing when clicked. These buttons are labeled "Backend pending" and are not yet active. Nothing is wrong, and no setting turns them on — they stay unavailable until the platform adds batch support. The selection is cleared when I switch to another view. Selections are per-view and per-session — they are not saved. Re-select your rows after switching views.
The toolbar above your table has two filtering tools. They work together and are both only about the table in front of you — they do not search the rest of your workspace.
documents.s: Narrow the current table with filters

documents.t: The Filter visible rows… box in the toolbar narrows the table as you type. It matches against whatever text is already loaded in the visible rows, in whatever script the text is written. Type a term and the table immediately hides rows that do not contain it. Clear the box and all rows come back. The filter box works on rows already loaded in the table. If the record you want lives in a different collection, it will not appear here — use the Search database… control at the top of the workspace instead. This text is not saved with the view. When you navigate away and return, the filter box is empty. For a filter you want to keep, use the filter builder below and save the arrangement as a view.
documents.s: The filter box — quick narrowing as you type

documents.t: Click Filter in the toolbar to open the filter builder. Each filter condition targets one field. Pick the field, then set a value with a control suited to that field's kind: Field kind What you set Text A word or phrase, typed in a text box Number A number, typed in a number box Date A date, picked with a date control Choice (single or multiple) One of the field's option values, picked from a list Any other field kind takes a word or phrase, matched against the value as it is displayed in the table. A row stays visible when the field's displayed value contains what you set. Matching ignores letter case. Comparisons such as greater-than, before and after, or ranges are not available in the filter builder. The table narrows as soon as you set a value, and the condition appears as a chip in the toolbar, shown after "filtering by". The chip names the field and the value, with a count of the rows that currently match, so you can see at a glance what is active.
documents.s: The filter builder — conditions by column

documents.t: Add more than one condition by picking another field in the filter builder. All active conditions must match a row for it to stay visible — the conditions work together. Each field carries one condition: setting a new value for a field replaces that field's earlier value. The filter box and the filter builder also compose: you can apply column conditions and then type in the filter box to narrow further.
Click the × on any chip to remove that condition. The table widens to include rows that now match. Click Clear — visible when at least one chip is active — to remove every condition at once.

You do not need a search term to use filters. If you want to survey a slice of your corpus — all records with a particular choice value, all rows that mention a particular place — open the filter builder, set your conditions, and browse the matching rows directly. No typing in the search box required.

Filters set while a saved view is active are remembered on that view. Open or create a view, set your conditions, and the next time you open that view your filters are already applied. See What happens to saved views after a re-import for how saved filters behave when a field changes.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The filter box does not find a record you expect. The box narrows rows already loaded in this table; the record may be in a different collection. Use the Search database… control at the top of the workspace to search across all collections you can access. A filter condition I set is gone when I come back to the table. You set the condition using the quick filter box, which is not stored. Conditions from the filter builder chips persist only when a saved view is active. Set the condition in the filter builder, then save the view. The filter box was matching rows, but a record I know matches is missing. The filter box works on text visible in loaded rows; a field that is not displayed as a column is not matched. Open the filter builder instead and target the specific field you want to filter on. I cannot find the Filter button. In a narrow window the toolbar lays its controls out on more than one line. Widen the window, or look for the button on the toolbar's following line. After I clear all chips, rows I expected do not reappear. The quick filter box may also have a term in it. Check the filter box in the toolbar and clear it. The filter builder does not show the field I want to filter on. The filter builder lists the fields configured for your collection. Contact your environment administrator if a field you need is missing from the filter builder.

Help is available without leaving the workspace, in two places.

The Help page (/app/workspace/help) lists the available guides grouped by topic — working with your data, finding and sharing, and importing. Open a guide to read it in place; each one answers a single task-shaped question in plain language. A direct link to one guide looks like /app/workspace/help/<guide-name>, so you can share a specific guide with a colleague.
Many controls have a small ? affordance beside them. Clicking it opens the matching guide in a drawer, right where you are working — so you can read the relevant help without losing your place.
If a guide does not cover your question, or a control is not behaving as you expect, that is worth reporting to your project's administrator — the help set grows as new behaviour ships.
documents.s: When help does not answer it

documents.t: When your source has two columns whose names are so similar that the platform cannot tell them apart as separate fields, the import stops before writing anything and shows you every problem at once. The report names each set of colliding columns so you know exactly what to fix.
documents.s: Fix colliding column names during import

documents.t: Each column in your source becomes a field with an internal identifier built from its name. Spaces, punctuation, and capitalisation differences are smoothed out so the identifier works consistently across languages and formats. When two differently named columns produce the same identifier after that smoothing — for example, "Author Name" and "Author-Name" both become the same field — the platform cannot accept both without overwriting one with the other. Rather than silently discard data, the import stops and reports every such collision in one message.

For each collision, the report names the identifier the columns would share and lists every source column that produces it — including which table each column comes from when your source has more than one table. If there are several collisions, they all appear together — the import never stops at the first one and leaves the rest hidden.

You have two options. Option 1 — Rename one of the columns in your source. Open your spreadsheet or data source, give the conflicting column a name that is meaningfully different from its counterpart, then run the import again. A small change like adding a word or removing an ambiguous character is enough. Option 2 — Leave one of the colliding columns out during the import review. In the review step, reject the proposed field for one of the colliding columns so only one of them becomes a field. The other column is not deleted from your source — if you need both, rename one there and bring it in with a later import. Your data is never changed or written while a collision is unresolved. The import stops entirely and waits for you to fix the source or adjust your review decisions before it touches anything.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The same column keeps appearing in the collision report after renaming. The new name still smooths out to the same identifier as the other column. Make the names more distinct — change more than capitalisation or a single punctuation mark. The collision report shows columns from different tables in my source. Two differently named columns in different tables feed the same collection and produce the same identifier. Rename the column in one of the tables, or leave one of them out during the import review. The import worked before but now shows a collision after I added a column. A new column you added has a name too similar to an existing one. Rename the new column to something clearly distinct before re-importing.

Rename a field label — giving a field a friendlier name after a successful import without changing your source. Understand what changed after a re-import — what the platform carries forward when the import completes successfully.

Relation fields connect a record in one collection to one or more records in another. For example, a "Text" record might have an "Author" field that points to a "People" record. Once a link is in place, it appears as a small labelled chip in the field. Linking happens in the Details view or directly in the table cell in the Table view — whichever you find easier to work with.

Open the record you want to edit, or click its cell in the table. Find the relation field (it shows existing links as chips, or says there are no linked records yet). Click into the field. A search box appears. Type part of the name of the record you want to connect to. Matching records appear as you type. Click the record you want. It appears as a chip in the field. The link saves immediately — there is no separate save step. In the table cell, the field also lists records from the target collection for you to browse before you type anything. You can add more than one link to the same field by repeating the search and pick steps. A record that is already linked is not offered again.
Open the record or click its cell. Find the chip for the link you want to remove. Click the × on the chip. The link is removed and the change saves straight away.
The Relations view shows every link for a selected record — both the links it makes and the links other records make to it. Select a link there to see its details, or to remove it.

A newly created row begins as a draft. Links can only point to active records. A row that is still a draft cannot be chosen as a link target until it is activated. While you are filling in a new row, its relation fields become available once the platform has created your draft — enter a value in another field first. From there you can link your draft to active records as you work. In the Table and Details views, link edits on a row that is still a draft are declined. Fill in the row's required fields and activate it; after that, links work normally everywhere. Links you added while drafting are kept.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The search box shows no results when I type. The target collection has no records yet, or your search term does not match any. Add a record to the target collection first, or try a shorter or different search term. The record I want to link to does not appear in the results. It may still be a draft — links can only point to active records. Activate that record first, then search again. The relation field in a new row is not editable yet. The platform creates your draft after you fill in a first value. Enter a value in another field and click out of it, then return to the relation field. The relation field is not visible in the Details view. The field may be hidden in the current view. Open Manage columns from the Table view toolbar and make sure the field is shown. I cannot add a link to my row from the table. The row is still a draft. Fill in the row's required fields and activate it, then add the link. The × to remove a link is not showing. Your role may not include edit access for this collection. Contact your environment administrator.

Build a knowledge environment from scratch without importing — how to create the relation field itself between two collections. Add a new record — the draft stage and how a new row becomes an active record. Make a field required — controlling which fields must be filled before a draft row becomes active.

When a field is required, a record cannot be saved while that field is empty. The platform will not let you activate the draft until you fill it in. Setting a field as required is always your decision. Your import never sets this automatically — the platform writes "not required" at creation and leaves the choice to you.

Open the collection whose field you want to change. Click Field Definitions in the toolbar or sidebar of that collection. (This opens the field configuration view for the collection — not the individual record.) Find the field in the list. Click its row to open its settings. Turn on Required. Save. From now on, any new record in that collection will require a value in this field before it can be activated. Existing records already in the collection are not retroactively blocked.

When you create a new record and blur out of a required field while it is still empty, the form surfaces a validation hint beneath that field. The Activate button stays greyed out until the required field has a value. You can save the draft with the field empty — autosave keeps your progress — but activation is blocked.
documents.s: What "required" means at the record level

documents.t: Required applies to new records you create. It does not affect records already in the collection. Your import never overrides this setting. If you mark a field required, re-importing your source leaves your setting intact (see Rename a field label for more on which settings survive re-imports). Removing the required flag works the same way: open Field Definitions, find the field, turn Required off, and save.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The Required toggle is not visible in Field Definitions. Your role does not have permission to change field configuration. Ask a project administrator to make the change. An existing record shows no required-field hint even though the field is empty. Required applies only to records created after the setting was turned on. Existing records are not retroactively blocked. The Activate button is still grey after filling in the required field. Another required field may also be empty. Check for other red-outlined or hint-bearing fields on the form.
Rename a field label — how to change what a field is called, without losing your data. Build from empty — creating tables and fields without importing a spreadsheet.

The left sidebar lists every table in your knowledge environment. When your environment has many tables, you can pin the ones you use most, gather them into named groups, and collapse or hide everything else — so the tables you need are always at the top, not buried in a long list.
documents.s: Pin and group tables in the sidebar

documents.t: Pinning adds a table to a Favorites group at the top of your sidebar. The table also stays in its regular group. Click the star next to the table's name in the sidebar — or open the table and press Shift+S. The table appears under Favorites at the top of the sidebar. To unpin it, click the star again, or press Shift+S while the table is open. Pinning is yours — it does not change what your colleagues see in their sidebar.

Named groups let you gather related tables under a heading you choose, so the sidebar reflects how you think about your work rather than the order the tables happen to arrive in. Press Ctrl+Shift+G (Cmd+Shift+G on Mac), click Add group at the bottom of the table list, or open the command palette with Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on Mac), type "sidebar", and choose Create sidebar group. The new group appears at the bottom of the table list with its name ready to edit — type a name and press Enter. Drag tables into the group, or drag them between groups to reorganize. Collapse a group by clicking its heading — only that group folds away, and the others stay open. Expand it again the same way.
Recent appears near the top of the sidebar and lists the five tables you opened last. Use it when you remember working in a table but cannot remember where it sits in your groups.

When you want more room for your table, press Ctrl+B (Cmd+B on Mac) to collapse the sidebar to a narrow icon rail. Each table is still reachable as an icon. Press Ctrl+B again to expand the sidebar back to full width.
documents.s: Collapse the sidebar to an icon rail

documents.t: If you want to undo all your pinning and grouping and start from scratch: Open the command palette with Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on Mac). Type "reset sidebar" and select Reset sidebar to default groups. This puts the sidebar back to its original layout. Your records and views are not affected — only the sidebar arrangement resets.
documents.s: Reset the sidebar to its defaults

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix Shift+S does nothing. Your cursor is in a text box, or no table is open — the shortcut pins the table you currently have open. Click the table in the sidebar to open it, then press Shift+S — or click the star next to its name instead. I cannot find the group I created. New groups are added at the bottom of the table list, and sidebar changes are saved only when you are signed in. Scroll the sidebar down. If the message near the bottom of the sidebar asks you to sign in, sign in and create the group again. Dragging a table into a group does not work. Tables listed under Favorites or Recent cannot be dragged — dragging works from a table's row in its regular groups. Drag the table's row from its own group. Or click the table once, press Space to pick it up, move it with the arrow keys, and press Space again to drop it. The sidebar looks different on another device. Your pins and groups follow your sign-in, but the sidebar's width and its collapsed or expanded state are remembered by the browser you used. Press Ctrl+B (Cmd+B on Mac) or drag the sidebar's edge to set the size you want on each device.
Choose between the quick search bar and Search & Read — finding records when the sidebar is not the right tool. Find help on a topic — more ways to get answers while you work.
Before an entry is visible to the public, you can see it exactly as a reader will — the same page, the same layout, the same references — so nothing about the published result is a surprise.

In the workspace Publish view. Pick a record from the row list and the public reader rendering appears beside it. The list shows a sample of the table's records for previewing; publishing always covers the whole table. While editing a record. The record drawer shows the reader view next to the editing form. After you save a change, the preview refreshes to the saved version. During an import. The import wizard includes a draft reader preview step, so you can check how approved rows will read on a public page. Previewing publishes nothing — no page goes live until you publish.

The preview is produced by the same renderer as the public entry page, so what you see is what a reader gets: the entry's sections, the field labels in your project's own wording, the references section, and any media. Published pages include only the fields whose visibility is set to Public; fields kept private or workspace-only do not appear on them. The preview reflects your entry as currently saved, not edits still in progress. A change to field visibility reaches the published page when you next publish — after adjusting visibility, labels, or citation rules, publish and preview again to confirm the result.
A record travels through three stages before a public reader can see it. Activation and publication are two separate steps — completing one does not trigger the other.
documents.s: Publish a record — and why activating is not publishing

documents.t: Stage What it means What to do Draft A work in progress. Your project colleagues can see it in the workspace, but it cannot be linked to other records and never reaches the public. Fill in the record; it is saved as you go. Activated A full record in your collection — linkable to other records and ready to publish. Still visible only in the workspace. Activate the record once every required field is filled. Published The record has a public page that anyone with the address can read. Publish from the workspace Publish view (publish access required). A record can sit at the Activated stage for as long as your project needs. Internal review, peer checking, or waiting for a companion record to be ready — all of that happens before you publish. Activation is the internal gate; publication is the public one.

Publishing happens in the workspace Publish view and covers a whole table at a time — every activated record in the table gets its public page built in one pass: Open your collection's table in the workspace. Select the Publish view from the view tabs. (If it is not listed, add it with + Add view.) Select Publish changes. The platform queues the work and shows you progress as it runs. When the job finishes, the receipt tells you how many records were published and whether any were skipped. Records that are already published are refreshed with your latest saved version, and draft records are skipped — so the same action serves a first publication, a single new record, and a table-wide update after a period of internal review. If Publish changes is unavailable to you, your role may not include publish access. See "Who can publish" below.

The public page shows the record as it was last published. When you change a published record — a text correction, a new media item, a citation update — the change reaches the public page the next time you publish. Edit, review, then select Publish changes again.

Publishing requires publish access, which belongs to your environment's administrators. Researchers whose roles include only edit access can add and activate records but cannot publish them. If you are ready to publish but do not have access, contact the administrator of your environment. They can either publish on your behalf or adjust your access.

Activation was designed as an internal milestone — a way to signal that a record is finished: every required field is filled, the record can be linked to other records, and it is ready for internal review. It is a checkpoint for your team, not a release to the public. Publishing is a deliberate, additional act because research is often collaborative and time-sensitive: a project may want to hold records until a companion table is complete, until a review is signed off, or until a specific date. Keeping the two steps separate means your team controls the moment of public release, independently of when individual records are finished internally.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A record is activated but does not appear in the reader. Activation and publication are separate steps; the record has not been published yet. Publish from the workspace Publish view, or ask a colleague with publish access to do so. Publish changes is unavailable, or publishing stops with a permission message. Your role does not include publish access. Contact your environment administrator to publish the records or to adjust your access. You changed a published record but the public page still shows the old version. The public page shows the record as it was last published; edits wait for the next publish. Open the Publish view and select Publish changes again. The publish receipt shows some records skipped. Skipped records are not ready for a public page — most often they are still drafts (not yet activated). Activate the drafts and publish again. If a record you expected to publish keeps being skipped, contact your environment administrator.

Your workspace has two search tools. They are intentionally separate — the right one depends on whether you want to jump straight to a record you already know, or browse, filter, and read across many records in one place.
documents.s: Choose between the quick search bar and Search & Read

documents.t: Open quick search from the Search database… control at the top of the workspace, or press Ctrl+Shift+F (⌘⇧F on Mac). A search panel opens over whatever you are doing. Type a word. Results appear grouped by collection, each one showing the record's label and the fields where your term matched. Select a result and the platform opens that record directly — whichever collection it lives in. The panel also controls the scope: search everything you have access to, search only the current table, or narrow the search to a single collection. Use quick search when: You want to land on one specific record and open it. You know roughly what you are looking for. You are in the middle of editing and need to jump to a related record fast.
documents.s: Quick search — for jumping to a known record

documents.t: Search & Read is a full search page you can dwell in. Open it from the quick search panel — the Open full Search & Read button at the bottom carries your typed term over — or from the command palette (Ctrl+K / ⌘K), where it appears as Search & Read. The result list is built for reading. For any result you can expand its content inline, open a preview panel beside the list, or click through to the record itself. You can page through the results and sort them by relevance, by recently modified, or by label. Filtering goes further than quick search. Switch to Advanced mode to: Scope the search to one collection, or leave it across everything you can access. Each collection carries a type badge, so you can see at a glance what kind of records it holds. Add conditions on field values. Each condition names a field, a match type (contains, equals, or starts with), and a value; a condition can also be negated. Conditions combine with Match all or with any. The page address encodes your query, filters, page, and sort order — paste the address to a colleague and they see the same results. See Share a search. Use Search & Read when: You want to look at several records, not only one. You want to apply filters — by collection, by a field value, by any combination — and see everything that matches. You want to share the search with a colleague. You want to read records without navigating away from the results.
documents.s: Search & Read — for browsing, comparing, and reading in place

documents.t: Quick search Search & Read What it does Jump to one record Browse and read many records in place Filters Scope only — current table or one collection Collection scope, field-value conditions, Match all / any Shareable address No Yes How to open Search control at the top of the workspace, or Ctrl+Shift+F (⌘⇧F on Mac) Open full Search & Read in the quick search panel, or the command palette (Ctrl+K / ⌘K) Best for "Find this record" "Show me everything that matches…"

If quick search finds results but you want to explore the full set, or you want to narrow it with filters: select Open full Search & Read at the bottom of the quick search panel. Your search term carries over. Switch to Advanced mode to add field-level conditions.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Quick search returns no results even though you know the record exists. Search matches against the fields your environment includes in its search configuration; your term may appear only in a field that is not covered. Try a word from a different field of the record. If it still does not appear, contact your environment administrator to review which fields are searchable. You cannot find Search & Read. It opens from the quick search panel or the command palette — there is no permanent menu entry. Your role may also not include access to workspace search. Open quick search and select Open full Search & Read. If the page reports an error or shows no collections, contact your environment administrator. Results show strings of letters and numbers instead of names. The collection has no display field configured, so results fall back to an internal identifier. Contact your environment administrator and ask them to set a display field for that collection.
Share a search — copy an address that reproduces your exact search and filters. What changed after re-import — using Search & Read to verify changes after an import update.

You can give any field in your collection a name that makes sense in your project's language — regardless of what the original source data called it. Your label is yours. Re-importing your source data never overwrites it.

Open the collection whose field you want to rename. Click Field Definitions in the toolbar or sidebar. Find the field in the list. Its current label appears in the Label column. Click the field's row to open its settings. Edit the Label field — type the name you want to use. Save. The new label appears immediately in the table columns, in the record detail view, and in filters.

When you first import a spreadsheet or data source, each field gets a label from your source — the exact column heading as it appears in the original file. For example, if your spreadsheet has a column called "Author full name", the label starts as "Author full name." From that moment on, the label is yours: What the import controls What you control The underlying field identity (which column this is) The label — what it is called in the workspace The raw data values Whether the field is required The field type detection (text, number, date…) Any notes or help text on the field Re-importing the same source updates the data but does not touch your label. Even if the column heading changed in the source, your label is preserved. The import may tell you a column was renamed in the source (it will show as "new" + "removed" in the delta), but it will never silently overwrite what you typed.
documents.s: What the import sets and what you own

documents.t: Your label has no length limit, but short and clear works best in table column headers. Renaming a label does not change any data. Records are not affected. Two fields in the same collection can share a label — the platform does not enforce uniqueness on labels. Unique field identities are managed internally.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The Label field is not editable. Your role may not have permission to change field configuration. Ask a project administrator. After renaming, the old name still appears in a filter chip. Filter chips may cache the name briefly. Refresh the page if the old name persists after a few seconds. Hard-refresh the browser (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+R). A re-import brought back the original source name. This should not happen: label is researcher-owned and never overwritten. If it did happen, it is a bug — please report it with the import project ID.

What changed after re-import — what the platform carries forward versus what it updates. Make a field required — other field settings you own that survive re-imports. Build from empty — creating fields from scratch where your label is the only name the field ever has.

A view is a named tab above the table that remembers exactly how you left it — which columns are visible, their order and widths, any pinned columns, active filters, sort order, row density, and row color rules. Open the view and everything is waiting for you. Views belong to the table and are visible to everyone working in your environment. When you create a view, your collaborators see it too.
documents.s: Save your table arrangement as a view

documents.t: A saved view stores: Which columns are visible, and in what order. Column widths, pinning (left or right), and sort order. Filter conditions and their values. Row density (compact, cozy, or comfortable). Row color rules. One thing it does not remember: the quick-filter text in the toolbar. That bar is a temporary per-session search — it is not saved with the view, so you always land on the full filtered result rather than yesterday's text.

Open the table you want to organize. Set up filters, columns, and sort the way you want this view to look. Click + Add view in the view tabs above the table. Type a name — something descriptive like "18th-century records with manuscript citations" — and select Create. The new tab appears. From this point on, any change you make while this view is active — adjusting columns, adding a filter, changing the sort — is stored on the view as you go. Changes are saved to whichever view is active — including the table's default view. If you want to experiment without changing what your collaborators see, duplicate the view first and work in the copy.

The default view is what opens when you first visit the table. Open the ⋯ menu on the view tab. Select Set as default. The default is shared: a table has one default view, and it applies to everyone in your environment, not only to you.
documents.s: Set a view as the default

documents.t: Because views are shared, editing one changes it for all your collaborators. Duplicating creates a separate copy you can adjust without touching the original. Like any view, the copy is visible to your collaborators — but your changes no longer affect the view your team relies on. Open the ⋯ menu on the view tab. Select Duplicate. The copy appears as a new tab named after the original, with "copy" added. Rename the copy so it is clear which one is the original. Work in the duplicate. When you are happy with the result, you can either keep both views or delete the duplicate once its changes have been folded back into the original.

Open the ⋯ menu on the view tab. Select Delete view and confirm. The view is removed for everyone in your environment. Talk with your collaborators before deleting a shared view — there is no undo. The table's default view cannot be deleted. To remove it, set another view as the default first.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Columns I arranged look different the next time I open the table. Views are shared — a collaborator may have adjusted the same view since your last visit. Or your changes were made on a different view tab. Check which view tab is active. For an arrangement collaborators will not change, duplicate the view and work in the copy. I changed a filter and now my collaborators see the change too. Views are shared — any change to a view reaches everyone immediately. Use Duplicate to make a copy before experimenting. I deleted a view and a colleague lost their work. Deleting removes the view for everyone. Check whether the view can be rebuilt from the column and filter arrangement. Going forward, agree with your team before deleting a shared view. The Set as default option is grayed out. The view may already be the default, or your role is read-only on this table. Look for a Default badge on the tab. If your role is read-only, ask your environment administrator. The Delete view option is grayed out. It is the table's default view — the default cannot be deleted. Set another view as the default first, then delete this one. Creating or changing a view fails. Your role is read-only on this table — creating and changing views needs editing access. Ask your environment administrator.
Saved views and re-imports — what happens to your views when you re-import your source data. Share a search — copy a link that reproduces a view or search for a colleague.

Your saved views are yours. A re-import never resets or overwrites a saved view. What you named it, which columns you included, how you sorted and filtered — all of that survives. There is one exception: if a field that a view referenced is removed in the re-import (because it no longer exists in your source), the view adapts gracefully.
documents.s: What happens to saved views after a re-import

documents.t: A saved view stores: Which columns are visible and in what order. Column widths, pinning, and sort order. Filter conditions and their values. Row density setting. The view's name. All of this is preserved across re-imports. Data values may update (a field's value in a record changes to match the new source), but the view's layout and filters are not touched.

If your source data no longer includes a field that your saved view referenced — for example, you removed a column from your spreadsheet before re-importing — the platform handles it gracefully: The view keeps working. The removed column is dropped from the display, but the rest of the view (its other columns, filters, sort) is unaffected. The import delta tells you. The re-import summary names the removed field and lists which saved views were affected. You do not have to discover this by accident. If the field comes back, a later re-import that includes the column again will restore it — and the view will include it again automatically.

If a saved view has a column that was removed: The view opens normally. The removed column is absent from the table. A notice at the top of the view (or in the views menu) indicates that one or more columns in this view are no longer available. Filters that reference the removed field are also suspended — the view does not try to filter on a field that no longer exists. You can update the view (remove the reference to the missing column and save again) or leave it as-is and wait for the field to be restored.

Sharing a saved view copies its URL. The recipient opens it with your layout and filters applied, subject to their own permissions. The URL does not embed data — it describes the view configuration only. See Share a search for how the URL encodes filter state.
documents.s: Sharing a saved view with a colleague

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix A column I pinned is gone from my view after a re-import. The field was removed in the re-import. Check the import delta summary for "removed" fields. Restore the field in your source and re-import, or update the saved view. Filters in my saved view stopped returning results after a re-import. The field being filtered on was removed, or the value that was filtered on no longer exists in the updated data. Open the filter chips and verify each one; delete and re-create any that reference removed fields. I see no notice about a degraded view but know a column is missing. The notice appears in the views panel; you may have dismissed it. Open the Saved views menu and look for any view marked with a warning indicator.

What changed after re-import — the full delta: new, changed, carried forward, removed, restored. Rename a field label — how your field configuration is preserved across re-imports. Share a search — copying a URL that reproduces a search or view for a colleague.
When you search for a record you know is there and nothing comes back, one of four things is usually happening. Each has a different fix.
documents.s: Find a record when search returns nothing

documents.t: Search matches against the fields your environment includes in its search configuration. If the word you typed appears only in a field that is outside that set, the record will not surface — even though it exists and you can see it by scrolling the table. What to try: type a word from a different field of the record — the label, a short description, or a name you know it carries. If that finds it, the original field is not in the search configuration. If no combination of words finds the record, contact your environment administrator and ask which fields are included in search.
documents.s: 1. The record's field is not included in search

documents.t: Search is forgiving about some diacritics and strict about others. Ignored (you can leave these off when searching): Breathings in polytonic Greek (smooth and rough) Iota subscripts Circumflex and grave accents Arabic vowel marks (short vowels / harakat) Not ignored (these still count): The acute accent — in Greek and in any Latin-script language The diaeresis (umlaut) This means: typing a word with no accent at all can miss a record whose stored form carries an acute accent. If you are searching a polytonic-Greek collection and your term has an acute accent, include it. If you are not sure of the accent, try a word from another field of the same record instead. Diacritic handling is part of your environment's search configuration, and individual fields can be set to match every mark exactly. If you have confirmed the accent is correct and search still misses the record, contact your environment administrator.
documents.s: 2. Accents and diacritics — what the search ignores and what it does not

documents.t: If your environment stores records with a native-script field, a transliteration, and a translation side by side, a search term in any of those fields can find the record — but only if those fields are searchable and have values. If you search with a transliterated form and nothing comes back: Open the record directly from the table. Check whether the transliteration field has a value. If the field is empty, add the transliteration — or ask your environment administrator whether the transliteration field is included in search. If the transliteration field has a value but search still misses the record, the field may not be in the search configuration. Contact your environment administrator.
documents.s: 3. The transliteration field is empty or not searchable

documents.t: When a collection has no display field configured, search results for that collection cannot show a record name. Each result shows a placeholder instead — "(unlabeled …)", or the collection's name with a "no display field" notice. The records are there and your search did find them; the problem is that you cannot recognize them. If you see this: Look for the type badge beside each result — it names the collection the result belongs to. Contact your environment administrator and ask them to set a display field for that collection. Once set, search results for that collection will show the record's name as the label.
documents.s: 4. Results show a placeholder instead of the record's name

documents.t: Symptom Most likely cause First thing to try No results at all for a term you know is in the record The field is not in the search configuration Try a word from a different field of the record Found nothing with a transliterated term but the record is visible in the table Transliteration field is empty, or not searchable Open the record; check whether the transliteration field has a value Term in native script finds the record but transliterated term does not Transliteration field not in search configuration Contact your environment administrator Search matches most Greek terms but misses a specific word Stored form carries an acute accent your search omitted Retype the term with its acute accent Results appear but show "(unlabeled …)" or a "no display field" notice instead of names No display field set for that collection Contact your environment administrator to set a display field Search panel reports "Search isn't enabled for this workspace yet" Search has not been switched on for this environment Use the table's filter box for the current table; contact your environment administrator for the workspace-wide fix

Choose between the quick search bar and Search & Read — which search tool to use and how to escalate from a quick search to a full filtered search. Share a search — copy a link that reproduces your exact search for a colleague.

When you run a search in the Search & Read section, the link in your browser carries the whole search — the words you searched, the filters, the sort, and the page you are on. Copy that link and send it; whoever opens it lands on the same search, with results filtered by their own access.
documents.s: Share a search so a colleague sees the same results

documents.t: Open Search & Read in the workspace and run your search — type your words and press Enter, or build filters in Advanced and select Search. Select Copy link, directly below the search box. The button confirms with Copied. Paste the link into an email, chat message, or document and send it. You can also copy the link from your browser's address bar — once the search has run, the address bar carries the same link. When your colleague opens the link: They see the same search words, the same filter conditions, the same sort, and the same page. They must be signed in to the same knowledge environment. They see only results their own access allows. If a collection is outside their access, its results are absent — sharing a link does not extend anyone's access.

A saved view (a named combination of filters, columns, and sort) has its own link: Open the view in your workspace. Select Copy current view link in the toolbar, or Copy view link in the saved view's menu. Paste and send. Saved views are shared across your knowledge environment, so a colleague with access to that workspace opens the same view — the same columns, filters, and sort. The link points to the view itself: if someone later edits the view, the link opens the edited version.

The search words (if any). Every active filter condition — the field, the match type, the value, and the Match all / any choice. The collection the search is scoped to, if you narrowed it. The sort order and the page you are on. It does not carry the records themselves. The results are live: whoever opens the link runs a fresh search against the knowledge environment as it is at that moment. A link shared today may return different results next month if records were added, edited, or removed. The link reproduces your search faithfully, not a snapshot of your data.
The same link works as a personal bookmark. Add it to your browser bookmarks, and you can return to the same search at any time without rebuilding the filters.

Symptom Likely cause Fix My colleague opens the link but sees fewer results than I did. Their access excludes some collections or records. This is expected — results respect each person's access. If they need access to a collection, contact your environment administrator. The link I copied is missing my newest filter changes. Search words and filters enter the link when the search runs, not while you type. Run the search — press Enter, or select Search in Advanced — and then copy. The link opens but the filters look different from what I sent. The link may have been truncated by a messaging app. Send it as a raw link rather than wrapped display text. A saved-view link shows a different layout than when I sent it. Someone edited the saved view since — views are shared, and the link opens the view as it is now. To keep a layout fixed, duplicate the view under a new name and share the copy's link.
Choose between the quick search bar and Search & Read — which search tool gives you a shareable link. Saved views and re-imports — what a saved view remembers and how it survives a re-import.
When a reader opens one of your published entries, the References section lists the evidence behind it — one row for each place the entry is attested.
documents.s: Read the references section on a published entry

documents.t: One row per occurrence. If a term is attested in twelve passages, the references section has twelve rows. Each row is independent. Your project's citation style. When you have declared citation rules for a collection, each row is rendered in your own scholarly format — author, work, locator (page, chapter, line), and any abbreviations exactly as your field uses them. The format is yours to control, not a fixed platform style. Paired editions. When an occurrence cites both a modern edition and an earlier one, the row bridges them — the primary citation followed by the paired locator, so a reader sees the equivalence at a glance. A quote, when the occurrence carries one, sits with its row.

Each row's text is chosen in order: your declared citation style first; if a collection has no citation rules, a plainer structural composition of the edition's locator fields; and the occurrence's own label as a last resort. A row always renders something — a missing edition never blanks the row. If the citations read roughly, the citation style for that collection has not been refined yet. Citation styles are tuned per collection (a scholar reviews a proposed style; an administrator applies it); the rows update on the next publish.
Use the draft preview to see the references section exactly as a reader will, before the entry is public — see Preview an entry before publishing.

When you import your source data a second time (a re-import), the platform shows you a delta — only what is new, changed, or different from your last import. It does not ask you to re-review decisions you already made.
documents.s: Understand what changed after a re-import

documents.t: At the top of the import review the platform shows a summary line like: Since your last import: 3 new · 1 changed · 147 carried forward Term What it means New A field or table that did not exist in the previous import. You need to review and approve it. Changed Something that existed before but is now different — a field type changed, a collection was restructured, or the source renamed something. You need to confirm the change. Carried forward A decision you made in a previous import that the platform has automatically recognized and kept. You do not need to act on these.

"Carried forward" means the platform compared your source to the last import and found no difference on a given field or collection — the same data, the same structure, the same decisions you already made. The platform keeps those decisions automatically and does not show them as review cards. You can expand the "Carried forward (K)" disclosure to see the full list if you want to verify what was carried.

A field or collection shows as removed when it existed in your previous import but is no longer present in the new source data. The field is not permanently deleted. Any notes, labels, or settings you made on it are preserved. If you bring the field back in a later import, it is restored — you get your previous settings back. The delta view names every removed field so you know exactly what changed. If a saved view referenced a removed field, the view keeps working but drops that column from its display (see Saved views and re-imports). The platform uses the words "removed" and "restored" — plain language that describes what happened. You will not see the word "inactive" or other system terms. Removed is removed; you can bring it back.
A field shows as restored when it was removed in a previous import and has come back in this one. Your previous settings — any label you gave it, any notes, your required flag — all return with it.

Your own edits — labels you renamed, field settings you changed, required flags you turned on — are yours and are never overwritten by a re-import. The only things a re-import refreshes are values that come directly from the source (the raw data itself), not your annotations and configuration choices. See Rename a field label for the full list of what survives a re-import.

Before the import writes anything, the wizard runs a practice run (sometimes called a dry run). It tells you how many records will be created, updated, or skipped — including how many are blocked by unresolved review items. With carried-forward decisions accounted for, a re-import of mostly unchanged data should show nearly all records ready, not blocked.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The import still shows a full review list as if it were the first time. The platform did not recognize this as a re-import of the same source, or an earlier import was never completed. Check whether the previous import was completed through Stage 6 of the wizard. Only completed imports produce a carried-forward baseline. A field I labelled is showing its original source name in the delta. The delta view shows source-side names for changed items; your label is preserved and will appear in the workspace once you confirm the change. Confirm or carry forward the item in the review. A field I know exists in my source is showing as "removed." The source column may have been renamed in the source system. A renamed column appears as a new column plus a removed column in the delta. Review the "new" items — one of them is likely the renamed version. Approve it, and your label will be carried to the new identity.
Rename a field label — which of your settings survive a re-import. Saved views and re-imports — what happens to your saved views when fields change.

This page explains what the platform records about you while you work, what it deliberately does not record, and the safety rules that occasionally hold content back. The bias throughout is to keep your project's content inside your project and to minimize what flows anywhere else. Read it when you want to know what the platform sees, when a feature seems to be holding a number back from you, or when a new chat panel appears and you want to understand what it is doing.

Your data stays inside your environment (Active) — your project's records, search queries, and edits live inside your environment's boundary. Researchers in other environments cannot see across it, and the boundary is enforced at the data layer, not by convention. Content-free activity records (Active) — when the platform records that an action happened (a search ran, an import finished, an assistant answered), it stores numbers and short labels — duration, row count, success flag — never the content itself. One-way redaction of sensitive text (Active) — where the platform must keep a record involving text you wrote, the text is replaced with a one-way fingerprint keyed to your environment; the original cannot be reconstructed from it. Text that looks like an email address, a phone number, or an identification number is dropped entirely — not even a fingerprint is kept. Small-sample protection on cross-environment statistics (Active) — a statistic computed across environments is published only when enough separate environments contributed to it that no single environment or small team could be identified from it. Below that threshold, the number is withheld. Tamper-evident activity records (Active) — the platform's activity records cannot be silently edited or deleted; the platform-level log links each entry cryptographically to the one before it, so any alteration becomes visible during routine verification by the platform operator. Chat conversations are not kept (Active) — a chat assistant keeps your conversation only for your current working session, or reads it once to extract the structured details you confirmed and then discards the raw text. No chat surface keeps conversations longer (see below). Data-protection assessment tracking (Active) — when deeper activity recording is switched on for an environment, the platform records that the environment's Data Protection Impact Assessment must be refreshed, and tracks that refresh to completion. Per-environment usage statistics (Active) — whether your environment records usage statistics about features such as in-form tips is a per-environment setting, not a platform-wide constant. Your environment administrator can tell you whether it is on.

If you have only a minute: Your project's data and the queries you type stay inside your project. They are not visible to researchers in other environments, and the platform operator sees only redacted aggregate numbers, never your content. Statistics computed across environments are published only when enough separate environments contributed that no single environment or small team of researchers could be identified from them. Chat panels keep your conversation only for your current session, or read it once to pull out the details you confirmed. No chat surface keeps conversations longer today. The record of who edited what stays inside your environment. It exists to give your editors and your administrator a clear history, not to surveil you.

Your researcher account. Sign-in identity, display name, role, permissions. Stays inside your project. Your edits. Drafts you create, fields you change, rows you activate. Attributable to you within your project, so editors and reviewers can see who did what. Chat conversations, within limits. A chat assistant follows the retention behaviors described below; the default keeps nothing beyond your session.
documents.s: What is recorded about your activity

documents.t: Your search queries do not leave your environment. Searches are matched inside your project. The platform-wide measurement layer never receives the words you typed — by design, it can only hold counts, timings, and one-way fingerprints. No content leaves your workspace. Platform-level activity records hold numbers and short labels, not the content of searches, imports, or conversations. Small-sample statistics are withheld. A cross-environment number with too few contributing environments is not published at all. Sensitive strings are redacted before storage. One-way fingerprint, keyed to your environment; text matching high-risk patterns (email addresses, phone numbers, identification numbers) is dropped entirely. The platform's activity records are tamper-evident. A background guarantee; no action needed from you. Much of this measurement is also switched off unless the platform operator deliberately turns it on — the platform's default posture is not to collect.
documents.s: What is deliberately not recorded or transmitted

documents.t: Two situations: Publication readiness. A draft, a row missing a required field, or a row in a review queue is not eligible for the public reader. The publish view shows what a record still needs before it can go live — see Preview an entry before publishing. Small-sample statistics. Where a precise cross-environment number could identify the behavior of a small group, the platform withholds it. This rule applies to platform-published numbers; it never hides your own data from you inside your workspace.
documents.s: When the workspace holds content back

documents.t: A chat assistant on the platform follows one of these retention behaviors: Session only (the default). The conversation exists for your current working session and disappears when the session ends. Nothing goes into durable storage. Extract only. The conversation is read once by an extractor that pulls out structured details you confirmed (for example, a summary of what you said you were importing); the raw conversation is then discarded immediately. Nothing longer. No chat surface keeps your conversation beyond the two behaviors above. Longer retention is not available today. The chat panel itself tells you what it records: it carries a visible notice stating that questions may be included in usage records and that no workflow changes happen through chat. The assistant can answer questions and explain what it sees, but it cannot change your data at all — it cannot approve, apply, publish, or delete anything. Actions happen only through the regular controls you click. One practical note: records belong to the project, not to you personally. Removing a researcher account does not remove the project's published records. If you are leaving a project and want to know exactly what account removal covers, ask your environment administrator.

Which chat surfaces are enabled, and what each one retains. Whether usage statistics — such as tip acceptance numbers — are being collected in your environment (see Efficiency tips for environment administrators). Whether a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) has been completed for the project. A DPIA names who can see what, for how long, under what conditions. Your administrator can find out its status from the platform operator and tell you what it covers. A worked example: suppose you notice a chat panel today that was not there last week. The right question to your administrator is two-part — "What does this panel retain?" and "Is the DPIA updated to cover it?" If both have clean answers, the surface is operating inside the platform's normal posture. If either is open, the platform's default — nothing kept beyond the session — is what applies until the answers land.
documents.s: What to ask your environment administrator

documents.t: Your project's database records, search index, and change history all live in their own slice of the platform. Operations that touch your project read from your slice. Operations that produce platform-wide numbers read from a separate measurement layer that holds counts and timings, never content. When you type into search, the query is matched inside your slice; the platform-wide layer can learn at most that a search happened, how long it took, and how many results it returned. Multiply by every action on every surface and you get the platform operator's view: a picture of motion without content. Researchers in another environment see less — they cannot see across the boundary at all.
documents.s: What the environment boundary means in practice

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix Where to escalate A statistic you expected shows no value, or is missing entirely. Small-sample protection withheld it: too few environments contributed for the number to be published safely. This is intentional. The number appears when more environments contribute. Your environment administrator; Tips and guidance. A new chat panel appeared and you do not know what it retains. The panel was enabled for your environment. Read the panel's own notice about what it records; if it is unclear, ask your administrator what the panel retains and whether the DPIA covers it. Your environment administrator. You cannot find what an administrator can see about your activity. The change history is the answer for "who changed what"; it stays inside your environment and is visible to editors and administrators. Ask your administrator to walk you through the change history for your account's actions. Your environment administrator. You want to verify that the platform's activity records have not been tampered with. The platform-level activity log is tamper-evident by design — verification is run by the platform operator, not the researcher. Ask your environment administrator to request a verification report from the platform operator. Your environment administrator.

Tips and guidance — the tip surface whose usage statistics are covered by small-sample protection. Efficiency tips for environment administrators — the tip surface from the administrator's side, including the per-environment setting for measuring tip activity. Activity measurement for environment administrators — what an administrator can configure about activity recording. Voice and vocabulary — how the wording you see is configured (not a privacy setting, but a related per-environment setting). Standards posture — the compliance framework that backs these privacy guarantees.

When somebody outside your project reads one of your records on the web, they are using the public reader — the reading-facing face of your knowledge environment, with stable URLs, scholarly citations, clean typography, and no editing controls. This page explains what the reader is, how a record reaches it, and how to preview a record before it is public. Read it when you want to know what a reader sees, when you are about to publish, or when you want to share a finished record with someone outside the project. The reader is configurable, so what your readers see depends on your project. The sections below describe how it works; your environment may use all of it or a subset.

Published reading layer — the reader reads from a separate, read-only snapshot of your data, refreshed when your project publishes something new. Readers never touch your working data. Maturity: Active. Stable, citable URLs — every published record has a stable web address that keeps citations valid even if the page is later reorganized. Maturity: Active. Limit: stability is per record; links to individual sections within a page are best-effort. Side table of contents — a navigation list down the side of the page that highlights where the reader is as they scroll. Maturity: Active. Limit: how fine-grained it is depends on how the record is sectioned. True-to-life preview — an in-workspace preview that renders a record exactly as a reader would see it, with no mockup substitution. Maturity: Active. Limit: the preview lives in your workspace; it is not a public address. Citations for media items — a media item can carry a structured citation in your project's citation style (defined in Citation Style Language, the same format reference managers use), rendered with the record's citations and ready to copy into a bibliography. Maturity: Active. Source-traced citations — citations on the record itself, built by tracing where each piece came from (source manuscript, prior publication, contributor) and rendering that chain. Maturity: Active. Limit: fidelity depends on the source links your project declared at import. References — one row per piece of evidence — every occurrence of the record in the sources gets its own row. Where the project has catalogued a modern and an early edition of the same source, the row bridges them into one scholarly reference (modern citation, then the early edition's locator and abbreviated editor); where the project has full citation styling configured, the row carries a formatted citation; and an occurrence with no published edition at all — a catalogued manuscript or fragment — still appears, shown by its own label. Quotes catalogued on an occurrence display beneath its row, and source citations the rows did not absorb appear once each, deduplicated, below the evidence list. Maturity: Active. Limit: how rich each row reads depends on what the project catalogued — locators, editions, quotes, and abbreviations are project data. Browsable indexes, switchable per project — beside search, readers can browse the whole corpus from an alphabetized index, and a project can publish more than one (for a multilingual corpus, for example by transliteration or by original script), switchable from the reader. Index rows are rich (transliteration, original-script form, and a short gloss together); a character rail jumps to a letter; large letter groups page smoothly. Maturity: Active. Limit: which indexes exist, the default, and what each row shows are configured by your project. Media on the record page — a published record lists its attached media — 2D images, audio, video, 3D models, and molecular visualizations — each item with its label and, where catalogued, a link to its source plus its identifier and version. Maturity: Active. Limit: only the media your project attached and published appears. Dark mode and reading-first layout — selectable text, a scholarly typeface, and a darker color scheme readers can switch to, remembered in their browser. Maturity: Active.

The reader is a separate layer from your workspace. The workspace is where you and your colleagues add, edit, review, and approve. The reader is where the world reads what your project has decided to publish. The platform builds the reader from a published snapshot — a separate, read-only copy of your data, refreshed when your project publishes something new. A reader visiting a page does not reach into your workspace; they read from the snapshot. Your editing speed is not affected by outside traffic, and a reader cannot accidentally see a draft.
documents.s: What the reader is, in one paragraph

documents.t: Readers do not have to search to explore. The reader offers a browsable index — an alphabetized list of every published entry — and a project can publish more than one. A multilingual environment commonly offers the same entries by transliteration and by original script; the reader switches between them from the controls at the top of the list. Each index row can show the transliterated form, the original-script form, and a short gloss together, so an entry is recognizable without opening it, and a character rail jumps straight to a letter. Which indexes exist and which is the default are set by your project when it publishes. See Browse entries by index.

Draft. You created it; the workspace knows about it; nobody else sees it (unless you preview it, below). Activated. You selected Activate. The record enters the main table and search results; other researchers can see, link, and cite it. The record is not yet public — activation never publishes by itself. Published. You — or a colleague with publish access — select Publish, for a single record or a whole table at once. The platform builds the record's published snapshot, and the public page goes live. Publication is its own step, separate from activation. Once a record is published, its snapshot refreshes automatically when something publishable changes — an edit to a published field, a media item added to a published record, a typo fix to a published citation. You do not trigger the refresh manually.
documents.s: How a record reaches the reader

documents.t: Use the preview to see exactly what a reader will see, before committing: Open the record in your workspace — a draft, an activated record, or anything you are working on. Open its reader preview. The preview renders the record exactly as a reader would see it — same layout, same fonts, same citations, same media rendering. During an import, the wizard's final step offers the same preview for newly imported records. Read it. Spot anything awkward. Close the preview. The record has not moved; you have only looked at it. The preview is a real rendering, not a mockup. If a citation will look rough in the reader, it looks rough in the preview too — that is the point. See Preview an entry before publishing. The preview reflects the current draft. The published page updates on the next publish, not instantly.

A reader visiting a published page can: Read and select text — lines are individually selectable for quoting and note-taking. Link to a published record through its stable web address; links to individual sections within a page are best-effort. Copy citations formatted in your project's citation style. Follow media to its source — each attached media item appears with its label and, where catalogued, a link to its source. Switch to dark mode (remembered in their browser). A reader cannot edit, comment on, or add anything. The reader is read-only by design.
documents.s: What a reader can do, and what they cannot

documents.t: Draft preview Published Who can see it You and colleagues with workspace access Anyone with the public URL URL Not a public URL — preview-only Stable, citable URL Visible on the public web No Yes Reflects edits On re-opening the preview after a change Only after the published snapshot next refreshes In short: the preview lets you see the reader's view without committing to it. The published view is what the world actually sees.
documents.s: Differences between draft preview and published

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix A record was activated but does not appear in the reader. Activation and publication are separate steps; the record has not been published yet. Publish the record, or ask a colleague with publish access to publish it. If you are unsure who publishes in your environment, contact your environment administrator. The preview shows different formatting than the table view. The reader renders from the published layout, not from the editing surface. Some fields render differently. This is intended — the preview is the truthful render. Adjust the record to match the reader layout you want. A citation for a media item shows placeholder or incomplete values. The media record's citation fields are missing or incomplete. Open the media record and complete its citation metadata. If the citation style itself looks wrong, contact your environment administrator. A media item attached in the workspace does not appear on the published page. The published snapshot has not refreshed since the item was attached, or the item is not part of what your project publishes. Wait a short interval and re-check. If the item is still missing, contact your environment administrator. You changed a published record but the change has not surfaced in the reader. The published snapshot refreshes automatically, but small changes are not instant. Wait a short interval and re-check. If the change is overdue, contact your environment administrator. A reader reports a broken section link they previously cited. The record was restructured; the record's own URL stays stable, but links to individual sections are best-effort. Share the record's stable URL and advise the citer of the new section location. If section links break often, contact your environment administrator. The preview is blank or shows a loading state that never finishes. The preview has not yet been built for this record, or it is failing to load. Refresh and retry. If the problem persists, contact your environment administrator.
